  125. Arabic sometimes forms words by analogy, as when one says “the clay turned to stone” or “the camel turned into a she-camel.” But this is an exception to the usual rule and should not be extended without clear evidence—especially to the common word “existent,” used of both God and possible things. More broadly, the author is discussing how words are formed from verbal sources. Such a source is normally an abstract meaning that can take different forms, unlike a fixed noun such as “iron.” — س قده

    ↩

  126. Earlier grammarians treated the verbal noun as the source from which derived words are formed. Later scholars instead located the source in the root letters shared by those words, while each word’s form expresses a different relation to that source. A derived adjective can express a relation to its source in several ways: directly, as striking relates to the one who strikes, or by an accepted kind of usage, as “iron worker” relates to iron or “sun-warmed” relates to the sun. If there is figurative extension, it lies in the meaning of the source, not in the grammatical form of the derived word. The critic’s examples therefore do not show that a rigid noun such as “iron” itself can be the source of a derived word; nor do they prove that the source must be literally present in its subject. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  127. The word “existent” can be applied to existence itself, just as “white” can be applied to whiteness and “hot” to heat. The standard for a derived word is that its source be either present in the subject or real in it in some other way; one specific relation need not always apply. — س قده

    ↩

  128. One version of the text adds “and,” but that reading is not sound. The examples are meant to explain figurative extension. The “source” is whatever makes the derived word applicable, not necessarily the technical source from which a word is grammatically formed. — س قده

    ↩

  129. The blacksmith is related to iron so closely that it dominates his thought and work; this can be described figuratively as his having a share in iron. It does not mean that merely imagining iron makes someone a blacksmith. — س قده

    ↩

  130. The image of the sun is present in the warmed water; “sun” can also be used for the sun’s rays. — س قده

    ↩

  131. If everyday word use is too ambiguous to establish philosophical truths, it is especially unreliable in cases that could mean relation, figurative realization, or literal presence. The author first says not to infer truth from common expressions, then notes that even ordinary usage does not always require a source to be present in its subject. If we examine usage carefully, he argues, it supports the conclusion required by reason. — س قده

    ↩

  132. Dawānī's point, as I understand it, is not that the reality of existence is itself a word or an idea. The source from which a word is formed belongs to language: one word may be formed from another. The reality of existence is neither a word nor a concept. How could it literally be the linguistic source from which the word “existent,” or its general meaning, is derived?

    It is a source in a different sense: the real existence from which the mind draws the concepts “existence” and “existent,” and to which those concepts point. We speak in a similar way when we call a real defining feature the source of the feature expressed in a logical definition.

    Dawānī also says that the source of the word “existent” can be something that exists through itself. This makes sense if he is speaking of the real thing named by the expression. It can also make sense if he treats the expression as a way of attending to the real thing, so that a judgment about the expression points through it to reality. That is how a term works in a statement about a whole class, rather than a statement about a nature considered only as a nature.

    The concept and the reality it describes are different, but not so unrelated that we cannot pass from the first to the second. A thing's appearance is that thing understood through one of its faces; otherwise a judgment about the appearance could tell us nothing about the thing.

    Existence, then, has both a concept and a reality. The concept is a name and a way of looking; the reality is what the name reveals. Some statements, such as statements about how words are formed, belong to the concept. Other statements, such as “it exists through itself,” belong to the reality. This is why the author says in The Beginning and the Return that the fact that a derived expression is a matter of thought does not make the reality from which it is drawn unreal. — س قده

    ↩

  133. Dawānī may mean that real existence, considered as the source of the word “existent,” becomes a general concept. But God’s being a true individual instance of “existent” does not make Him a universal or a particular in the ordinary logical sense. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  134. The reply is that knowledge of God is innate: God is so clear and radiant that His very fullness of light hides Him from us. Everyone knows himself through direct awareness, though this awareness has degrees, and direct awareness of oneself cannot be separated from awareness of one’s source. This kind of inborn knowledge is enough to explain our use of words for God. If God is also the one who gave words their meanings, there is no difficulty.

    ↩

  135. One possible answer is to interpret “source” broadly enough to include both God and possible things. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  136. The critic says that sometimes “existent” is derived from “existence,” and sometimes from the relation to existence. The reply is that a derived word and its source must correspond in both sound and meaning. If “existent” means existence itself, it is derived from existence; if it means something related to existence, it is derived from that relation. The author may also use “source” to mean what makes the word applicable, not only a verbal noun. — س قده

    ↩

  137. “Blacksmith” consistently means someone related to iron, never iron itself, so it is not a close parallel to “existent.” Dawānī tries to give “existent” one broad meaning: either what produces effects or what has existence. But the first meaning has no trace of existence in it, while the second does not fit “existent” when it means merely “related to existence.” Real existence can be a subject in its own right, but then “existent” is no longer a general term shared by God and other things. The author’s point is not merely that common usage determines the meaning; it is that reason supports the ordinary meaning, unless proof shows otherwise. — س قده

    ↩

  138. This is a strong objection. If God is real existence, then existence is real; the fact that it has no many instances inhering in essences does not make it a mere mental idea. A nature is real if even one real instance exists. Some later philosophers try to say that possible existences are not themselves instances of existence, since the outside world contains only essences, and that God is an incidental instance. But this does not resolve the problem on the author’s terms.

    ↩

  139. Dawānī’s discussion seems inconsistent: he says that if existence is considered on its own it has no existence in something else, but elsewhere says it cannot exist apart from another. The issue is more than whether existence is fundamental; it is whether it is real at all. — س قده

    ↩

  140. As noted earlier, the argument confuses a concept with its individual reality. Calling God “particular existence” is only a technical expression for those who treat existence as conceptual.

    ↩

  141. The alternatives may concern whether the critic consciously distinguishes a thing’s being qualified by something from that quality’s inhering in it, or confuses the two. The author uses both expressions at times without distinction. More precisely, a quality’s inherence is the feature that makes predication possible; being qualified is the relation expressed by the judgment. A second-order concept may exist only in the mind while applying to something in reality, as with possibility or “thingness.” — س قده

    ↩

  142. A subtle case does not require a more obvious case in which the essence and its attribute have separate existences. To say that a quality is added to essence requires only that the essence exist; it does not require an existence separate from that quality. A quality added to existence, by contrast, requires an independently existing subject.

    ↩

  143. The author is distinguishing the mystics’ “unity of existence” from the view that existence and existent are one reality whose levels are many. On the first view, essences are real and many, while existence is a mental concept; beings are united only by being related to existence. The author argues that this does not yield the deeper unity of existence. On his own view, existence is a real, graded light: each particular existence is a level of it, and relations between levels express the one reality. The parts of the world are therefore united more deeply than by contact or dependence. At the highest level of the created world, the complete human being gathers the forms of all other kinds of being, as a final form gathers the earlier forms within it. All things depend on that final form for their full actuality, and it in turn depends on God, the One who sustains all. The changing stages of the world are gathered in an enduring reality, just as the same human being remains while bodily conditions change.

    ↩

  144. Those who say that a collection exists as one thing usually mean that all its members together exist, not that the arrangement of the members forms a separate reality. Some later scholars, including al-Lahiji, do treat the whole as a distinct existent; some proofs of God’s existence rely on that assumption. — س قده

    ↩

  145. Otherwise, one possibility would be preferred over another without any reason. — س قده

    ↩

  146. A cause must precede its effect. This applies to the whole understood as a single reality, not to all the members simply taken together. See al-Lahiji’s Shawāriq. — س قده

    ↩

  147. In this example the Necessary Being alone is the complete cause of the first effect. Once that effect exists, the pair is a whole; no further cause is needed to make the whole.

    ↩

  148. If the argument is only a trick, the author’s criticism stands. If it comes from a philosopher who sees God as necessary in every respect, it may mean that God is present at every level of existence and with every existent, yet has no separate essence at any one level.

  149. The argument would be sound if it said that both unity and multiplicity are caused, rather than saying multiplicity is possible in relation to necessary existence. — س قده

  150. Dawānī treats existence as a mental concept and holds that everything outside the mind is an essence. So he interprets “God is pure existence” to mean “God is pure existent”: since existence has no real instance, God cannot be existence. This is only a verbal dispute. In reality, a thing is either real existence or an essence; there is no third kind.

    ↩

  151. This approach reverses the true one. On the true view, an essence is existent by being one with a real level of existence, from which the concept of existence is drawn. The essence itself has no separate counterpart in reality; it is indeterminate and disappears into the existence that makes it real. Dawānī instead denies any real instance of existence and says that an essence becomes existent by being one with the concept “existent.” The two views are opposite, though Dawānī’s rejection of a real split between essence and existence may seem close to the truth. His view still leaves possible essences as the real things, and it cannot explain why they deserve to be called existent.

    ↩

  152. On Dawānī’s account, the concept of existence is shared and mental, while its application to real existence is either figurative or based on another use of the word. This would make God have existence twice: as His own reality and as an instance of the shared concept. But the same problem applies to Dawānī’s account, since he treats God’s real existence as an instance of the general concept.

    ↩

  153. The author is presenting the consequence of Dawānī’s view, not endorsing it. If God’s essence is not a real instance of existence, then saying He is an existent means only that an abstract concept applies to Him. But Dawānī also says that existence does not inhere in an essence. His own account therefore faces the same difficulty. — س قده

    ↩

  154. A particular human being is a nature of humanity surrounded by individuating features. The universal nature and its particular instance are not two separate existences. Likewise, “existent” applies to particular existence as an external predicate, not as a quality added to it. — س قده

    ↩

  155. The discussion of mental analysis here does not yet answer Dawānī’s second objection. It only shows that a particular existence and the general concept do not amount to two separate existences in God, as a possible thing can be analyzed into what does not resist existence and what does.

    ↩

  156. An essence, in the technical sense, is a bounded nature that can be thought of as universal or particular and that does not in itself require existence or nonexistence. Any limited nature is an essence. Existence, knowledge, power, life, and the divine names point instead to unlimited reality, so God has no essence in that technical sense. “Essence” can also mean more generally what makes a thing what it is or answers the question “What is it?” — س قده

    ↩

  157. The concept of existence relates to its real instance as an essential feature relates to the thing it describes: it reflects that reality, unlike a merely added quality. But the real nature of existence cannot be present in the mind without being changed into a concept. So the shared concept does not literally become part of the individual reality it describes. This is why Sadra can call existence a second-order concept while holding that existence itself is real.

    ↩

  158. These are the possible essences, which are dependent features of actual existence. — س قده

    ↩

  159. One might ask how Dawānī can say that “existent” is identical with a possible essence when he denies that a real or mental instance of existence is present in the essence. The strongest version of his view is that both God and possible things are sources from which the concept “existent” is drawn: God is that source through Himself, while a possible essence is such a source only because it has been brought into relation with its maker. But this relation is itself existence. What makes God and possible things existent is therefore the reality of existence, even if one avoids that name.

    ↩

  160. “Confusing kinds of predication” here is not the familiar fallacy of attaching an unrelated condition to a subject. The mistake is to confuse strict, meaning-based predication with ordinary predication. A concept is always itself in meaning, but it is not always an actual instance of itself. — س قده

    ↩

  161. The true subject of metaphysics is unrestricted real existence: existence in its full reach, not limited to any one nature. When philosophers call “unrestricted existent” the subject of the science, they mean the real nature as it appears in its instances, not the universal concept alone. The fallacy comes from leaving out that qualification. — مره

    ↩

  162. The argument also risks confusing what is actually present to the mind with what the mind could analyze if it were present. A thing may be analyzable in principle even if it cannot exist as a mental image. This is another case of treating an abstract description as though it were the reality itself.

    ↩

  163. The concept of existence is self-evident; its real nature is the light and manifestation itself.

    ↩

  164. The author uses blackness as an example of a simple reality that can be present in itself or in another thing. Blackness also evokes darkness, which helps suggest how all distinctions and traces of other things disappear within the simple, luminous reality of existence.

  165. There are three levels of oneness: the oneness of necessary existence, already proved; the special oneness of real existence, which will be discussed later; and the oneness of God as the sole deity and creator, established here. The first does not by itself prove the third. For example, the Muʿtazilites held that human beings act independently through their own power; another view would say that God created the first intellect and then left it to act on its own. That is not the philosophers’ position. For them, God alone gives existence; separate intellects, souls, and natural causes are only means through which His generosity and giving reach things. Only what is free of potentiality can give existence. — س قده

    ↩

  166. In short, nothing comes to exist by itself. All things receive existence from God, both when they first come to be and for as long as they continue to exist. The act of bringing something into being follows from the reality of existence itself. — س قده

    ↩

  167. The sun analogy is only a starting point; God’s relation to things is not literally like sunlight. Sunlight spreads over surfaces and visible things, while the light of existence reaches everything sensed, imagined, conceived, and beyond. Sunlight touches only the outer surfaces; existence reaches into the depths of things and makes them depend on itself. Sunlight is not aware, while the levels of the light of existence are living and aware. Sunlight also fades and has other lights beside it; the light of the Real never fades and has no second.

  168. No matching term in the digitized text · preserved for completeness

    The word sayb means “giving” or “gift.”

  169. Grammatically, “alike in nature” describes the elements; “in different places” describes how they are situated. — س قده

    ↩

  170. They would be separated in the sense of occupying different places, but could not remain permanently apart after first being naturally joined. Otherwise there would be empty space in the worlds from which they came and into which they moved, ruptures and joins in the spheres, and heavy bodies moving outward. All these results are impossible.

    ↩

  171. “First” refers to the beginning of the separation, and “return” to its end. The argument concerns all worlds, not only their elements. A permanent division of two bodies of the same kind—for example, two suns or two spheres—would require permanent force, but the heavens are not moved by force. They would have to return to natural unity, which would also bring the earlier contradictions. Ordinary individuals of one kind in our world are different: each individual passes away, while the kind continues only through successive individuals. The argument also rules out a world naturally made of many separate individuals from the start: their like parts would have to be separate too, yielding multiplicity without any unity.

    ↩

  172. Natural place is essential to a body of a given nature and cannot vary. If the places themselves joined together, place would have to move and have another place of its own. Nor can what is the center become an outer edge. — س قده

    ↩

  173. Such a union is possible in itself, even if the physical arrangement of the world would prevent it from actually occurring because it would require empty space or a break in the heavens. — س قده

    ↩

  174. Avicenna argues that no different natural movement or sensible quality means there can be no naturally different bodily world. One might object that the same effect can arise from different causes—for example, heat from fire, anger, movement, or the sun. The reply is that this resemblance holds only at a broad level; on closer examination, the kinds of heat differ. Even “evenness,” which applies to four, eight, and other numbers, is an abstract feature with no separate instance in them. Abstract features follow the things from which they are drawn, and one concept cannot come from wholly different things precisely as different. — س قده

    ↩

  175. The author first divides straight movement into three kinds, then revises this to a two-way division: movement either toward or away from the center.

    ↩

  176. The nineteen qualities are nine familiar simple tastes, four active and passive tangible qualities, three qualities of hearing, sight, and smell, and three qualities sensed indirectly. It would be more precise to list the basic tangible qualities individually. The author’s point is that the natural world has an ordered governance; as the active intellect governs this world in the philosophers’ account, so a governing power oversees the elemental world. — س قده

    ↩

  177. If nature moved a thing into a higher kind before completing the lower kind, there would be a sudden jump in its qualitative or substantial development. The philosophers reject such leaps, as they reject a sudden jump in place. This is the principle that a lower possibility must be fulfilled before a higher stage can be reached; it applies to the ascending order of things. — س قده

    ↩

  178. A sense and what it senses are correlatives and correspond to one another. A rational soul therefore has every sense that is fully represented in rational being.

    ↩

  179. Indirectly sensed things include quantity and relation. Avicenna names the most common and clearest examples. Geometrical body is counted among bodily qualities, and boundaries are included in shape. Movement and stillness are mentioned after movement and its divisions: stillness is the absence of movement in a place where movement is possible. They may also be counted as qualities in their own right, or as general kinds listed after their specific kinds. — س قده

    ↩

  180. The author gives an argument about the world’s unity that can speak to several philosophical approaches. His own view goes further than connection or contact: the parts of the world are genuinely one in existence, where what distinguishes them is the same reality that they share. Every earlier form is contained as potential matter within the final form of the complete human being, which gathers the forms of the world. What is indeterminate exists only through what gives it determination, so the world is fully actual through this final form, which itself exists through God. In another way, the kinds of beings are gathered into their higher principles and ultimately into the light of the human kind. The world’s cycles and changes pass, while this deeper unity remains. — س قده

    ↩

  181. The argument relies on one kind of dependence: a body causes another body only with a relation of position, and position cannot relate a body to something that does not yet exist. — س قده

    ↩

  182. An intellect must act and so would produce a bodily shadow or effect in the world; a soul must govern a body. Either way, separate intellects or souls would imply other bodies, whose existence has already been ruled out. The author sets aside the first claim because it would make the argument only persuasive, not conclusive.

    ↩

  183. Parts can be classified in four ways. They may share one external existence and be parts expressed in a definition, such as broader kind and defining feature; or be distinct parts considered in thought, like mental matter and form. Or they may have several existences: parts separated by position, such as parts of size, or external parts like real matter and form. — س قده

    ↩

  184. One might object that broader kind and defining feature are parts of what a thing is, not of its existence. The reply is that “existence” here includes the thing’s being established as real. The priority meant is priority in the thing’s basic reality, not necessarily temporal priority or efficient causation. — س قده

    ↩

  185. Parts of size may be posterior in actuality, since the mind first has a magnitude and then divides it. But magnitude itself makes division possible; that is what is meant by its parts. A point or an immaterial thing does not contain such divisible parts. Also, if a body had parts of size but no parts in its definition, it would still have matter and form, and therefore broader kind and defining feature, contrary to the premise. — س قده

    ↩

  186. The proof that dimensions cannot be infinite is this: one body cannot be the cause of another body of the same kind in a way that makes one prior to the other. If the Necessary Being were an extended body and caused another extended body, neither would be prior by nature. Each would have to be both cause and effect, leading to an unending series of bodies. But dimensions cannot extend without limit. — س قده

    ↩

  187. “Nature” here means either a kind essence or real existence. If a quantitative part were necessary in itself, it would still be only potential as a part, since a part of magnitude exists only as divisible magnitude. That conflicts with being necessary in itself. The clearer proof is the earlier argument that God, as Necessary Being, cannot have any limiting boundary.

  188. This and the following proofs rule out every kind of part, not only parts of size. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  189. The dependence here is dependence for existence, not just dependence in the way parts support a whole. Even if the composite whole were called necessary, the possible part’s existence would depend on the other Necessary Being; since existence is prior to essence, the whole would depend on that being for its existence. That contradicts the premise.

    ↩

  190. You might object that many wholes are made of parts that are not themselves the whole: a human being is made of animal and rational, and a house of roof and walls. But in a definition such as “animal, rational,” the parts are naturally related to the whole; a house is made of material of the same kind as its parts. The case of necessary and possible is different: the aspects of being free of nonexistence and being open to nonexistence have no such shared nature. — س قده

    ↩

  191. The same objection can be raised here—that a whole depends on its parts while a possible thing depends on God for existence. The reply is the same as in the previous note. — س قده

  192. First, if something simple in thought were made of matter and form in reality, it would also have broader kind and defining feature in thought, which contradicts its supposed simplicity. Second, a thing simple in reality need not be simple in thought: accidents, for example, can be analyzed into broader kind and defining feature. This distinction preserves the two directions of the argument: simplicity in thought rules out external matter and form, though external simplicity alone does not rule out mental parts. — س قده

  193. The broader kind depends on defining feature to become a definite kind of being, whether in the higher intellectual realm or in our own thought. A broader kind is incomplete and vague; it has no separate “lord” or ruler of its own, and cannot be pointed to in thought as a complete thing.

  194. Predication requires unity in existence and multiplicity in meaning. If the parts were pure existence, there would be no distinct meanings to predicate. If they were essences other than existence, there would be distinct meanings but no common existence in which they could be one. If they were a mixture, one aspect would be only unity and the other only difference; neither would allow the required predication. Ordinary broader kind and defining feature can be predicated because they have a separate, accidental existence in the mind. But God’s essence is pure existence, not a mixture of existence and essence. — س قده

    ↩

  195. “Dividing defining feature” includes a feature that classifies a species, a subclass, or an individual. The phrase covers the possible divisions of essence: a composite species such as human, a simple species such as prime matter, or a most general kind. — س قده

    ↩

  196. The simple species is mentioned to cover every possibility. In essences, it has no broader kind above it and no species beneath it.

    ↩

  197. The previous proof began by denying essence and its dividing features. This proof begins from the fact that the Necessary Being is the highest degree of existence, so He cannot be indeterminate and await a feature that makes Him definite. — ط مد ظله

  198. The phrase “becomes definite as an existent” applies to both kinds of feature. A species does not need a classifying feature to be pointed to by the mind; the reference may instead be to the inner senses that imagine or remember particular instances. — س قده

  199. “Nature” here means nature as realized in individual things. No one would think that the bare nature itself—the subject of a general proposition—is divided into individuals.

  200. True oneness is when a thing is one in itself, with no second feature serving as the basis of its unity. Non-true oneness applies when several things count as one because they share something: Zayd and ʿAmr are both human, while horses and cows are both animals. Humanity and animality are true unities; the people or animals that share them are one only in this derived sense. True unity may itself be the Necessary Being's self-subsisting oneness, or a unity added to a possible essence.

  201. To be fair, the thinkers who offer these examples mean us to attend to the ways they bring the subject closer, not to the ways in which the comparison fails. Consider the soul and the body. God is above all literal comparisons, but the example can still teach us something. The body lives through the soul, which sustains it and is its inward life, although the soul is not simply a thing located inside the body or standing outside it. In a far higher way, the world lives through God's sustaining presence. He is the source that holds together every life and every bodily form. He does not enter things as a body enters a space, nor is He outside them as one separate object is outside another.

    As the verse says, “In every thing there is a sign pointing to His oneness.” The highest examples can therefore reveal God's light and show how everything depends on the One. Seen in that way, all faces bow before the Living, the Sustainer. A thing, considered as a sign or face of its source, reveals that source through its own existence. God shows Himself through Himself and remains unlike what He creates.

    We must not carry over the ways in which the human soul differs from God. The soul needs the body in certain respects, is affected by it, and comes to be with it. None of those features belongs to God. For that reason, after using an example, some writers immediately correct themselves and pray, as the Persian verse puts it: “You are beyond all that I can imagine or say; dust upon my head and upon my comparison!”

    Still, the right response is not to ban all examples. Prophets used them, and the Qur'an does too, as in the verse that begins “The likeness of His light is as a niche.” There is a reason for this. Our minds, tied as they are to imagination, struggle to grasp meanings without giving them a picture. This reflects the correspondences between the levels of existence. When the intellect says that God is light—meaning an ever-living reality that exists through itself—the imagination pictures a dazzling ray. When it hears that He encompasses all things, it pictures a vast physical space. When it hears that He is above every other light, it pictures something literally higher, or the sun outshining the stars in daylight.

    A mind trained in careful proof need not accept these pictures as literal truths. It can reject the imagination's mistake while keeping the meaning that the example was meant to suggest. It knows that God's attributes are far beyond bodily pictures. But consider the person whose thought is still ruled by imagination. Such a person's pictures may be as confused as dreams, whereas the images used by disciplined reason and spiritual insight can be like truthful dreams: they invite us to move from the picture to the reality it points toward.

    If imagination were denied any examples, and the mind were given only abstract meanings, the two powers would quarrel. Imagination would refuse to follow reason. It would be like inviting guests to a table and feeding only some of them, though all need food. This may help explain the poet Rumi's saying that the images by which God's friends are drawn onward are reflections of the beautiful faces in God's garden. — س قده

    ↩

  202. The author himself is cautious about the analogy: the soul's relation to its body is not the same as a shopkeeper's relation to a shop. The analogy is limited and does not make the two relations identical.

  203. The proof can be put briefly: anything from which some feature can be denied is made definite through both an affirmation and a negation. Whatever is formed from affirmation and negation is composite. By contraposition, what is simple in reality has nothing denied of it; it is all things. This is not ordinary predication, as in “Zayd is human” or “Zayd is standing.” Ordinary predicates include both their positive and negative boundaries, which would make a simple subject composite. Here, only the positive, existing perfections of things are present in the simple reality; it has every perfection and rules over every perfection. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  204. To say that the perfectly simple reality “is all existences” is to give the reason in the description itself: it includes every perfection because it is simple. It is existence through and through, unmixed with any separate essence or absence. The word “as” in the passage means “because,” much as in the Qur'anic instruction to remember God because He has guided you.

    The point is many perfections within one reality. One level of existence, through its undivided reality, contains the perfections found across all other existences. It can do, in its one reality, what the many do in their different ways. The statement does not mean one reality spread among many things, as some readers mistakenly suppose. They hear that the simple reality is “all things” and object that stones and clay would then have to be Necessary Being. That turns the claim around. It is not saying that every particular thing is the perfectly simple reality.

    The spread of unity across the many belongs instead to God's all-embracing gift of existence, received by each thing according to its capacity. Spiritual writers have often described this second view. The first view—seeing all perfections gathered in divine simplicity—is the one the author regards as especially his own. He finds only a brief anticipation in Aristotle and says elsewhere that he has not found anyone who fully knows it.

    Yet writers on spiritual knowledge also speak of seeing the many within the one and the one within the many. Perhaps the author means that they have not made the same distinction rigorously. We should not assume that their language means something crude when other, clearer statements in their works may explain it. A verse of ʿAṭṭār's Conference of the Birds seems to hint at the point: all are before Him, yet He precedes all; all are seen through Him, and He is seen through all.

    Mīr Dāmād also writes that God is all existence and entirely existence, all beauty and perfection and entirely beauty and perfection; everything else is a flash of His light, a trace of His existence, and a shadow of His reality. This may mean that everything called “existent” gets that description from Him, whether we speak of His own existence or that of others. But that alone is not the complete claim at issue. The fuller argument and the careful closing of its difficulties remain, in this commentator's judgment, the author's achievement. — س قده

  205. The “not being” that contributes to composition is not a separate existing thing. The deepest composition is a positive feature together with the denial of some perfection. Existence and existence are not two different kinds; the second aspect is absence, possibility, or a boundary. Even “impossible existence” has a kind of conceptual thinghood while remaining nonexistent. A possible thing likewise combines its essence, which is not itself existence, with the absence of other perfections. The word “Zayd” points to his existence, essence, and the perfections he lacks. Pure existence has no such lack or essence and is therefore not composite. — س قده

    ↩

  206. We are speaking about what exists in reality, not simply about an idea formed in the mind, although the author's wording might suggest otherwise. The Necessary Being has no foundation but pure existence. Lower levels of existence are different: what makes them the particular levels they are includes their limits, lacks, and absences.

    Someone may object that we cannot say lower existences are made up of existence and nonexistence, since whatever actually exists is still an instance of existence. That objection confuses unrestricted reality with its limited levels. What makes a limited being this particular being is not another positive existence added alongside existence. Its limitation is real as a boundary, not as an independent thing.

    Our honored teacher offers a simpler route to the result: God possesses every perfection found in anything else, and none of those perfections can be denied of Him. Necessary existence means that His existence cannot fail under any condition. Were it bounded, existence would be absent beyond the boundary, and so He would not be necessary without qualification. He must therefore be unrestricted. No way of existing, and no perfection belonging to existence, can be excluded from Him.

    ↩

  207. The same point appears in the first journey: negating “horse” of “human” is not pure nothingness, but a denial made of an existing subject. This answers the objection that a negative statement has no subject and therefore no aspect that could be compared with its positive aspect. In this context, a negative statement with an existing subject functions like an affirmative statement whose predicate is itself negated. — س قده

    ↩

  208. The immediate point is clear, but elsewhere in The Four Journeys and in The Witnesses the wording reads differently: “What makes a thing what it is differs from what makes it true to say that it is not another thing.” The conclusion does not follow plainly from that wording. The question is why a human being is not a horse, not why a human being is not human.

    The author explains the point in The Secrets of the Verses. The meaning of a negative statement cannot be exactly the same as the meaning of a positive one, even when each is said in relation to something else. What the statement refers to is distinct from the meaning of the relation itself. Restricting a statement by that reference does not change the underlying nature of affirmation or denial. If the affirmation of A meant exactly the denial of B, affirmation itself would become denial. A thing would not be itself, which is impossible.

    Put another way, suppose we deny the existence of ʿAmr of Zayd. If Zayd's own existence, considered together with its limits and lacks, were itself what made that denial true, it would be a combination of positive existence and absence. That is impossible in the case now being discussed. But if we denied ʿAmr's existence of Zayd's existence simply as existence, we would be making a thing other than itself: for in this argument we are considering existence as existence, not as one limited share of it. If it were only a particular share that was absent, the denial would rest on that share's limitation; that is the first case again. — س قده

    ↩

  209. “Unrestricted existence” and “restricted existence” here anticipate the mystics' terminology below. A kind's definition limits it to a narrow range of perfections; a possible essence is likewise a bounded mode of existence. If one existence included the perfections of a human being and a celestial being, it would not be the restricted kind “human.” — س قده

    ↩

  210. “A fully realized kind” means a kind complete in existence, not merely a concept with a complete definition. “Animal” is conceptually definable but remains an open, broader kind; further perfections can be added without losing the name.

    ↩

  211. Philosophers usually use “unrestricted” and “restricted” for mental concepts. Mystics use the terms for real existence itself, in the sense of a reality that has breadth and encompasses its manifestations. In this usage, the mystics' unrestricted existence is like the philosophers' “simple existence, which is all existences.” — س قده

    ↩

  212. This explanation begins from the fact that the unrestricted is the source of the restricted and contains the perfections of its effects. The earlier approach is, however, more far-reaching, for it also establishes true unity and other important conclusions. — ط مد ظله

    ↩

  213. The author gives another form of the argument. Rather than begin with “the simple is all existences,” begin with the claim that the source and final end of all existence is their perfection. A giver of good cannot lack the good it gives, and a thing's end is its own perfection. If the end lacked that perfection, reaching it would not be completion but a change into something else.

  214. A long line loses no part of line itself when separated into shorter lengths; it loses only endpoints and points of division. Those limits are not lines, and points are a different kind of thing from lines. — س قده

    ↩

  215. The verse about water more directly illustrates unity spread through multiplicity than multiplicity within unity. “Living” is explanatory here, not restrictive: every thing has life and awareness in its own way. — س قده

  216. The flow of existence through things does not mean that the divine source acquires the changing attributes of what it flows through. In this sense, its light shines through every reality, and nothing veils it except its own majesty.

  217. Every thing glorifies God through His own praise: all existents reveal His names and attributes. Their praise is not merely evidence of a maker, as theologians often say; every good and beautiful existence belongs first to God and only then to a thing's particular form. The editor connects this with the saying, “I have not seen a thing without seeing God before it.” The Qur'an speaks both of creatures praising and of God praising Himself. “Understanding their praise” means awareness that they are aware; embodied people cannot attain this knowledge of knowledge unless they are freed from bodily veils. — س قده

    ↩

  218. The two examples point to a distinction between an attribute that is purely real and one that is real but necessarily involves a relation. Attributes, whether used of God or created beings, fall into four kinds.

    First are negative attributes: statements that deny something. Even a word without an obvious “not,” such as blindness or inability to read, can express the absence of sight or learning. With God, an example is holiness, understood as freedom from defect. Second are purely relational attributes, such as being the knower of an object or having power over it, when we mean only the relation itself. Third are real attributes that involve no relation and do not require one, such as life, necessary existence through oneself, or a knower's awareness of itself. Fourth are real attributes which are not relations in themselves but necessarily involve one, such as knowledge of another thing or power over it. Zayd's knowledge of the sun, for example, is a form or quality in his mind. It is not itself the relation between Zayd and the external sun, but it gives rise to that relation: he is the knower of the sun.

    We can now see why negative attributes are not identical with the essence of the one described. Otherwise the subject would itself be an absence. Someone may reply that the reality to which a negative description applies can still be the divine essence, just as God's real positive attributes are identical with it even though their meanings differ. But absence and negation have no independently existing instance. An existent thing cannot itself be an instance of nonexistence. It can only be the reality from which our mind draws a negative statement. A positive meaning, by contrast, can be truly realized in something that exists. And a general nature can exist through the individual that genuinely realizes it.

    Another objection is that God's negative attributes often deny a negation and therefore affirm something. The answer is that negation, considered simply as negation, still has no positive reality corresponding to it. Any positive force in the double negation comes from the existing thing that makes the statement true, not from negation as such.

    Purely relational attributes are likewise not additional parts of the essence. If they were identical with it as relations, the subject would be nothing but a relation. The same question and answer apply: a real being allows us to describe a relation, but the relation considered as a concept is not the being itself.

    How, then, can a negation or a relation count as an attribute at all? Because the mind does not require every true description to be a separate object existing outside it. The description must be grounded in how matters really stand. For example, “being a universal kind” can truly be said of human beings or horses even though universality is something the mind recognises rather than a physical part of either animal. Thus the real, positive attributes of God, both purely real attributes and those that imply relations, are identical with His essence. The negative and merely relational descriptions are not additional realities in Him. — س قده

    ↩

  219. Here the author means the concept of God's sustaining relation, under which all His particular relations to things can be gathered. God's true existence sustains unrestricted existence, which some call the all-embracing mercy. Unrestricted existence, in turn, sustains limited beings in a dependent way. Besides these realities, we can speak of relational sustaining power: an idea that gathers all the relations philosophers say are additional to the divine essence.

    Could the author's meaning be different? Perhaps the realities from which we draw these relational attributes all return to the true, life-giving relation just described. On that reading, they are its aspects, and it contains them as the many divine names and attributes are understood to be contained within divine oneness. Each name would be the one named, considered through a particular perfection, as the mystics teach.

    But this reading does not fit what the author says a few lines later: these relational attributes come after both the one related and the things related to Him. The true sustaining power does not come after what it sustains. It belongs to the very first level of reality and precedes everything through that precedence. Indeed, as the act of connecting one thing with another, it cannot simply be judged identical with the essence or an additional part of it in the way an ordinary attribute can.

    Finally, the sustaining relation spoken of as an attribute means giving and upholding existence. If we instead take “self-sustaining” to mean only standing through oneself, it would no longer be a relational attribute in the sense used here. — س قده

    ↩

  253. The word “therefore” seems awkward here. The statement “whoever knows what Necessary Being means” appears to refer to our understanding of a concept, not to direct knowledge of the reality itself. Three readings are possible.

    On the first, the opening describes the beginning of knowledge and the later phrase about the reality of existence describes its perfection. But this goes against the plain sense and does not work: the author explicitly says that the first kind of knowledge leads us to affirm that a Necessary Being exists.

    On the second reading, both parts concern direct knowledge rather than concepts. The word “knows” can suggest acquaintance with a particular reality, and “meaning” can refer to the reality meant rather than a general idea. This reading makes better sense of “therefore.”

    The third, and strongest, reading takes the opening as perfected knowledge through concepts, and the later passage as a step beyond that to direct awareness. The use of “meaning” supports this. Moreover, the author does not say that understanding the meaning of Necessary Being is the same as directly seeing that being. He offers a proof. Someone wholly absorbed in direct awareness would not need a chain of proof in the same way. The proof is quoted from an earlier knower; the later statement is the author's own.

    On this third reading, someone first understands the general concept of Necessary Being. When the mind considers existence as such, it finds that one kind of existent does not need to be related to anything else in order to be called existent: that is God. Another kind exists only through its dependence on something else; indeed, its existence is that dependence. Understanding this distinction leads the mind to affirm a Necessary Being, because dependent beings exist and need their source. The author then takes a further step: if knowing the concept can lead to affirming God's existence, how much stronger is direct awareness of existence itself?

    An objection remains. Direct awareness normally seems to concern either knowing oneself or knowing something that comes from oneself. God is neither the knower's self nor an effect of the knower. How, then, can one know Him directly? The reply is that one can know through the passing away of one's sense of separate self in what is known. No alien existence need stand between the knower and the reality of existence. What makes them distinct is not utterly foreign to what they share. Forgetfulness creates the distance; the passing away of self-centered awareness removes it.

  261. An objection might be made: the author often says that what distinguishes one thing is the same reality through which it agrees with other things. Why does he reject that argument here so sharply?

    The answer is that the principle belongs to existence, not to separate essences or the concepts used to define them. In the definition of a kind, the feature that distinguishes it from other kinds is not simply the general nature that it shares with them. The feature and the general nature are distinct in thought. Their existence, however, can be one, especially in a simple being. Here the proposed difference would be between the reality of existence and the mere standing of a concept. That is no more a shared way of being than saying that a limited thing is distinguished from existence by its limiting essence.

    Besides, the principle is helpful only if the higher level contains the positive reality of the lower level within itself. If the higher level lacks something that must then be added to it, it would be composed of what it possesses and what it lacks—or of a shared core and an additional part. That is exactly what divine simplicity rules out, as the cited sermon teaches.

    We have also seen that real existence is itself will, power, and the other perfections. If a supposed “existence” had to receive those attributes as additions, we would no longer be speaking of real existence without qualification. The comparison between the two would break down. There would be no shared reality on which to base the claim that the same thing both distinguishes and unites them. This is a matter of argument, not merely a choice of words. — س قده

  262. The difference between created things and God does not mean that pure existence is deprived of existence. The difference is in their attributes and limits, not in their being cut off from the source.

Existence is not a number or a part of a number. — س قده

  264. Philosophers use this expression for the forms of things said to be present in God's prior knowledge and care. Their existence is through the all-embracing existence of God.

    The author uses the expression for the level of the divine names and attributes. That level is particularly vast, because there the differences of meaning can be as numerous as we please without dividing the underlying reality. It is called the lordly realm because, on one mystical view, the divine names and attributes govern the kinds of things. The rising of the light for it is, in this sense, a new “day.”

    Or the words may mean the real divine names and attributes. The concepts we use are names of those names; the real name is existence itself considered through one of its divine perfections. God is revealed to Himself through His essence, through His names and attributes, and through the places where those attributes appear.

    In the level where the names are one, each is present in every other according to its existence. Every reality there contains the meaning of every other. It connects possibility with necessity and multiplicity with unity. The gathered disclosure of the names is called mercy at the level of attributes. When God's command “Be” appears through His actions in the ordered and varied world, that is called mercy at the level of acts.

  276. The “thing known” here means the form directly known in knowledge that works through representations. A few lines later the author calls it “a pure, luminous existence of awareness.” His point in this principle is that what is immediately known is the known form, rather than the external thing known only through that form.

    He is not yet giving a complete division of everything that can be known, nor distinguishing all the kinds of knowledge. The difference between direct presence and knowledge gained through forms will come later.

    So it would be a mistake to object that a material thing known through direct presence can exist for the knower exactly as it exists in itself.   277. “Known” is used broadly here, for all four kinds of knowledge. In the earlier passage it meant the intellect's universal object, in contrast to sensory perception.

  278. An objection arises about the features said to accompany a person, such as Zayd, when he is understood intellectually. Are these features general ideas of shape, position, and the like? If so, they do not affect what Zayd is, for the Zayd understood as a universal is simply a human being. A general idea of shape is not an actual bodily shape. Whether we think of that idea together with the human concept makes no difference to its existence. What matters in bodily life is a shape or position actually belonging to matter, not the abstract concept of one.

    Or are these features meant as spiritual counterparts of bodily organs? Aristotle's description of the intellectual human being may suggest this. In such a being, the 'hand' is whatever enables action and the 'foot' whatever enables movement. If someone could act through intention alone or cross the earth without walking, that power would serve as a hand or foot in the relevant sense. Philosophers do not regard such spiritual features as obstacles to understanding.

    A third possibility is that the body's actual shape, position, and color accompany the knowing soul and what it knows. Yet the soul and its knowledge do not disappear when the body disappears, still less when its position, shape, or color changes. Those features cannot be essential to intellectual knowledge.

    The answer is a fourth possibility. The features of material individuals can be included in the intellectual reality to which those individuals belong, but in a higher and unified way. The many particular beings are expressions of one reality. They are, so to speak, the spreading rays of a light or the broad bases of cones whose points meet in a higher source. Their shapes and positions therefore have their grounds in that higher reality, not merely in detached abstract concepts.

    The human being understood by the intellect is one simple, immaterial existence. It gathers the truth of every human individual into a more complete unity. Its individuals express that unity within multiplicity. The author accordingly says, in his discussion of the soul, that to understand a human being intellectually is to grasp a human being free from any particular size, place, or position, without leaving out any of its defining powers or members. The intellectual human being has head, face, eyes, stomach, hands, and feet, but all are understood in a way shared by many individuals.

    Elsewhere he says that removing every accompanying feature is not a condition of understanding a thing. The intellect can understand a human being with all its features—quantity, quality, place, position, time, shape, and members—so long as these are understood in a general intellectual way. He compares this with divine knowledge of particular things.

    He does not mean only that the spiritual meanings of these organs are included in a higher unity. He also means that the many features appearing in individuals have their reality within it, although not as features confined to one particular body. The reference to God's knowledge of particulars makes this clear: not an atom in heaven or earth escapes that knowledge. The author's wider rule is to hold together God's transcendence and the scriptural language describing His closeness, without reducing God to a body. — س قده

  290. The argument can be set out as follows. Either we are directly aware of the disruption in the particular part of the body where pain occurs, which is the point to be proved, or we know that disruption through an image of it. If through an image, where is the image? If it is in the same affected part, two images of the same kind would occupy one place. If it belongs to the soul at the level of understanding, it would be a general concept, not this particular pain. If it is present in another power, such as sight, then anyone who had the same image in sight ought to feel the same pain. That does not happen. Looking at an injury may produce distress, fear, or another kind of suffering, but it does not produce the particular pain of the injured part.

    An objection remains. Why could one form not belong to the soul in its lower, touching power, or arise in a power associated with it, while the other belongs to the bodily organ itself? They would then be present in different ways rather than two things occupying one place.

    The answer is that at the level of touch the soul is precisely the touching power. That power works by spreading through and receiving impressions in the body. A form present in it is therefore present in the affected organ as well. The difficulty returns.

    Someone might object that knowledge requires the known form to be separated from matter. But that condition applies to knowledge obtained through a mental form, not to direct awareness of a thing through its own presence. The Illuminationists likewise hold that material bodies are directly present to the Light of Lights.

    Why, then, can we not know every bodily object directly, without lifting it into a mental form? Because direct awareness occurs when a thing is present to itself or when it is aware of what depends on it as its effect. Other physical things are neither ourselves nor effects produced by us. Our bodily powers and their conditions, however, belong to us in that intimate way. — س قده

  303. The commentator connects this claim to the author's view that even acquired knowledge is grounded in immaterial forms. Their distance from us is what makes them seem universal or indistinct. — ط مد ظله

  304. The “lights” mentioned here are the higher principles of the material kinds of things. They give those kinds their standing, much as the soul sustains the body through its presence. They are also the fullness of those things: not merely the ideas by which we describe them, but the realities from which their existence comes and toward which it is directed. A thing's full reality must be united with it in some way. Otherwise it could not be its completion or its goal.

    The point is to prevent a misunderstanding. The author has said that material things, taken in themselves, cannot be direct objects of knowledge. Someone might conclude that the higher principles therefore do not know them. But the higher lights are directly present to themselves and are the complete realities of the material things that depend on them. To have those complete realities present is also to have their less complete forms present. This is not how an image in our mind relates to the thing pictured. Our image neither causes the thing to exist nor joins it in that close relation between many things and their single source. A mental image therefore gives us a weaker knowledge of its object. Even so, the thing is disclosed through the image, just as what we see indirectly is disclosed through the visible form immediately before sight. Nothing need be left out of that disclosure, but it is still not the same kind of knowledge as the higher presence. We can also understand the higher lights more broadly, as including material things within their own sources in a fuller and simpler way.

    I would go further. Material things are dark and not directly intelligible to us. In relation to the higher principles, and especially to the First Principle, they are directly known. This is knowledge through presence and action, even if it is not the same as God's knowledge of Himself. A material thing's presence in matter prevents us from grasping it fully, since our awareness does not surround matter and all it contains. But the One who encompasses matter knows it through that very presence. Indeed, the thing is present to the cause that necessarily produces it more fully than it is present to the matter that receives it. Even the thing's presence in its receiver falls within the knowledge of that cause.

    The divisions, absences, and passing away that keep us from direct awareness do not limit the Principle that encompasses everything. It is present in what has passed, what is present, and what is yet to come. It remains constant through all things that change and disappear. In relation to that all-embracing presence, separation does not mean exclusion, absence does not mean ignorance, passing away does not mean loss, and darkness does not hide what is there. A prayer says that no dark night, stormy sea, or enclosed darkness conceals anything from God: for Him, darkness itself is light.

    Existence, moreover, is what is most fundamental in everything. The way one existence differs from another does not set it outside the reality they share. So the material things need not first be stripped of matter before they can in any sense know their principles. The Qur'an says that nothing exists without praising God. Their knowledge is simple rather than the combined, reflective knowledge we ordinarily call thinking.

    There are, then, two senses of life. In the narrower sense, a living being can perceive and act: touch is the lowest kind of perception, and movement by choice is the lowest kind of action. This belongs to animals and higher beings. In the wider sense, life accompanies existence itself and, in truth, is one with it. Knowledge can likewise mean the special awareness that belongs to living creatures, or the deeper knowledge that accompanies existence wherever it is found. With this distinction, we can understand how the author denies that material things are themselves knowledge in one sense while still holding that existence and knowledge are inseparable in another. — س قده

  305. Someone may object that everything, even an immaterial intellect, exists through another—namely God. All things depend on Him so completely that their existence in themselves is also their existence through Him. Would the argument then imply that nothing except God can know itself? No. ‘Existing for another’ here means existing in another as in a material subject. ‘Another’ means matter in the broad sense, including underlying matter and the subject in which a quality exists. The eye, for example, does not see itself merely because it is a power present in a bodily subject. Its dependence on the soul is a different matter. A second objection is that Sadra elsewhere holds sight, hearing, and the other powers to be immaterial.

    Should they not therefore know themselves? The principles quoted here are those of the earlier philosophers, whom Sadra follows at the beginning of the inquiry but not at its end. They treated these powers as lodged in matter. Even in Sadra's account, the powers depend strongly on bodily expressions; for this reason their perception requires the presence of matter or something like it. They are not immaterial in the complete way that intellect is. Still, someone who holds that a wholly immaterial sensible form would itself be sensing, sensed, and the act of sensing can also hold that a sensory power freed from gross matter knows itself at its own level.

    Its sensing belongs to the soul, since the soul gathers all its powers; the object sensed is the form disclosed by that power. The power makes the soul manifest, and the perceived form is the power's own disclosure.

    ↩

  306. The commentator corrects the claim that the philosophers used a faulty argument. They did not reach the conclusion by combining the two claims above; they established each direction separately.

    ↩

  307. “Can be understood” includes even a very general way of being understood, such as being known as existent, necessary, or possible. — س قده

    ↩

  308. The argument runs as follows. If a being free from matter were understood by something else, it would exist for that other knower. It would then seem to depend on something else as a subject in which it was present, contrary to the assumption that it was wholly free from matter.

    An objection: why must knowing it place it inside the other being? Could it not be known directly through presence? The answer is that this proof belongs to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school, who treat another being's understanding as the reception of its form. On their account the thing understood in itself must have the same existence as the thing present to its knower. Its very being would then be received in the other, which is the difficulty the proof exposes.

    A second objection: universal forms are present in our intellects and are called immaterial. Does this not show that an immaterial form can exist in a subject? Here the word 'immaterial' is being used in different senses. For those philosophers, a universal form is free from external matter and its bodily features, but it is still received in the soul as its subject. On the author's own view, understanding happens through the soul's encounter with the higher realities of kinds, or through union with them. It is not the reception of an image in a subject.

    But then, the objector continues, must a universal form know itself? That sounds absurd if we think of the concept of a horse. The reply is that a concept and its intellectual existence are not the same thing. The author does not say that the meaning 'horse' becomes a thinking person. He says that its luminous intellectual existence is united with the knowing intellect. At that level it is intellect and soul, and its existence is aware of itself.

    Another proposed proof appeals to a pair of related terms: knower and known. If a separate being is known in its own right, perhaps it must also know in its own right, because the two relations stand on the same level. The author has used an argument like this elsewhere to explain the union of intellect and what it understands. But the commentator doubts that the relation alone proves union. Cause and effect are also related, as are mover and moved. Their relations require them to stand in a corresponding order; they do not require them to be one being. If every related pair were one and the same, we would collapse opposites into a single subject in the same respect.

    Nor does saying that the known is 'known in relation to a knower' solve the difficulty. The concepts 'known' and 'knower' remain different. Their difference does not by itself prove that two existences are involved, but their connection does not by itself prove that there is only one. A further argument is needed. One possible approach is to understand the relation as an actual connection of presence and illumination, not merely as a comparison between two concepts. This would explain a kind of union in disclosure without reducing a higher being to a lower one.

    To be fair, this is probably the author's real intention. He is not relying on related words alone. His deeper point is that a directly understood, luminous reality has no existence or activity apart from its being disclosed. Even if we supposed that nothing else existed, its own existence would still be a form of understanding. With no other object present, that understanding would be understanding of itself. This differs from an effect, which cannot remain an effect if its cause is removed from consideration. A being known in itself does not require another knower in that way. In actual understanding, moreover, something known in actuality requires an intellect knowing in actuality. That is the proper force of the relation between them. — س قده

    ↩

  319. For example, fire's basic nature is a cause of heat. The source of heat is present before the relation called “causing heat” and before the heat itself, so knowing that source reveals the effect. — س قده

  320. The effect does not identify its specific cause. Its essence, possibility, or existence considered as related to its essence is too indefinite to do so; it points only to some cause. A specific cause, by contrast, brings about its particular effect.

  321. The commentator holds that reasoning from cause to effect gives certainty. Reasoning from an effect to a cause gives certainty only when it proceeds from a common consequence with no separate cause of its own; otherwise it does not amount to a demonstration. — ط مد ظله

  322. The author first says that knowing a cause is one way to know its effect, then adds that things with causes can be known only through their causes.   323. In a detailed account, God causes the many levels of existence in an ordered sequence, from the higher and nobler to the lower. The author presents this as common ground among the different views. — س قده

  324. This is directed at followers of Suhrawardi’s Illuminationist school, just as the preceding point addresses Aristotle’s school. A voluntary act, in the philosophers' account, is preceded by knowledge, desire, will, and power.

  325. The ancient philosophers may have meant that God does not know other things eternally because no other things existed eternally.   326. Most theologians hold this view, even if they avoid calling God's knowledge “universal” or treating it as something added to His essence.

    ↩

  327. This note attaches to the claim about things being known “in reality,” and points out that the sources describe two ways of speaking about their prior status. Some copies also give the total number of views as eight. — س قده

    ↩

  328. Another way to organize the views is to ask whether God's knowledge comes before things. If it does, it may concern all things, as in Plato's view, or only some, as in Thales' claim that forms exist in an intellect present to God. — س قده

  329. The author adds that the Muʿtazilites themselves may not need a separate proof of God's knowledge, since they deny that His essence has attributes.

  330. “Higher minds” here means the higher level of knowledge. But how is this view different from that of the Muʿtazilites? They say that essences have a fixed reality apart from all existence, whether outside the mind or in it. The view under discussion separates essences only from existence in the external world. Once we place them in higher minds, they have existence there. That seems no different in principle from our ordinary mental knowledge of essences that have no external existence.

    The reply is that both views go wrong if they assume that a thing's essence has a reality of its own alongside existence. Existence is what is fundamental. An essence is considered a “thing” through the mind's way of understanding existence, wherever the essence is found. There are not two independent realities—existence on one side and the essence's fixed being on the other. Even when our mind treats them as two, the difference is one made by thought. Removing existence in a definition does not give us an essence that stands on its own: its being understood still depends on existence. What appears as a receiver and something received is, in reality, existence considered in two ways.

    The author's immediate point, however, is narrower. The essences are said not to have their own particular existences, and he rejects the idea that their fixed standing can be wholly separate from existence. His answer will say that, although they lack their own proper existence, they are present through God's existence. If the point had merely been that an essence does not exist independently of existence, one could have replied that its presence through God is compatible with its having only a dependent, conceptual standing—just as when the thing has its own limited existence. We must not overlook that distinction. — س قده

    ↩

  331. The Arabic word translated here as “recoil” means to shrink away from or keep one's distance from something.

    ↩

  332. Ibn Arabi uses “Be” as God's word. In the Nahj al-Balāgha, God's word is also described as His act; that act is the existence that flows through things. — س قده

    ↩

  333. The reports about things praising God before their worldly existence describe them as existing for God, not as independent beings. Their praise in that state is their recognition that dominion belongs to Him. — س قده

  334. This is the Ashʿarite position. In another discussion, Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī interpreted the claim that knowledge “follows” what is known as a claim that the two must correspond, with the known object setting the standard for that correspondence.

    Here, by what is known first, the author of the view means an essence considered simply as what it is, apart from being made what it is by some added act. A thing's essential features are not put together by a further maker. By divine knowledge he means the simple, undivided existence of those things at the higher level, an existence that has no separate individual features of its own. To say that knowledge follows the known is to say that this knowledge takes on the distinction belonging to the fixed realities. Considering what a thing is comes before considering whether it has one kind of existence or another: we understand what belongs to it in itself before what belongs to it through something else.

    The best answer combines both ways of speaking. What is known comes first as regards the distinct character that knowledge expresses. Knowledge comes first as regards undivided existence. And what is known comes after knowledge when it appears as a particular thing in the created world.

    But why would the fixed realities choose darkness, unbelief, or misery? Everyone seeks what is good and what makes them happy, in every realm. The reply is that at the level under discussion “evil” is evil only in what the word means, not as a harmful reality actually existing there. Evil, in its realized form, is what opposes a thing's existence and well-being, while good suits it. There is no separate existence at that level for such good or evil to act in this way. Every essence seeks an existence here in which its own nature and what follows from it can appear. It does not seek to have that nature abolished.

    Think of the letters alif and dāl. The straightness of alif and the curve of dāl belong to what makes each letter the letter it is in the writer's mind. When they are written, they must appear with those features. An alif is not asking to become a dāl, nor a dāl to lose its own shape. In the same way, the fixed realities appear according to the identities they possess. — س قده

  335. Just as each fixed reality gives itself its own character, God's one command brings to light what is already implicit in those realities. God gives generously; each being appears according to its own nature.

  336. The comparison is that God knows His essence, names, and attributes as they are, just as He knows the forms of those names—the fixed realities. It also invokes the principle that knowing a cause entails knowing its effects.

  338. “Common usage” here means the ordinary way theoretical thinkers use the phrase. The note is not claiming that philosophical truths can be established by popular opinion.

  342. The union of intellect and intelligible has two senses. In God's simple, perfect knowledge, the One contains all intelligibles without division. In detailed knowledge, God's light is united with each known reality without leaving its own level.

  347. The criticism concerns the arguments taken together. To say that relations exist because there are real things from which we can understand those relations is hardly a strange invention. Many Muslim thinkers have said much the same thing. So that claim alone cannot be the reason for calling this view utterly absurd.

    Perhaps the criticism instead refers to the idea that relations are like “the fangs of monsters”: things imagined but not found outside the mind. Yet when the author calls their existence “assumed,” he does not mean that the mind is free to imagine them without any basis. He means something like the way we speak of things in a general statement that remains true whether or not we are thinking of any particular example.

    Once we consider a relation, it can exist as a distinct idea in the mind. Before anyone thinks about it, however, its existence in the world is simply the existence of the real things from which that relation can correctly be understood. Those things provide a sound basis for the idea.

  348. Some descriptions, such as blindness, can be understood from one subject alone. Other relations, such as brotherhood, require two subjects. The relation between knower and known belongs to the latter kind.

  349. God's power is actual, not a mere capacity waiting to act. The created effect may be potential before it exists, but this does not make God's power potential.

  350. “From outside” means from beyond God's essence. Avicenna's account is that the forms arise from God, as an effect from its source, rather than being received from something external. — س قده
