  351. The author means an attribute that comes to a thing from outside, so that the thing already exists as a subject before receiving it. In that case, receiving the attribute requires a power to be affected; here that means matter. The resulting composition is therefore real, not merely a distinction made in thought.

    One might object that a separate intellect also receives existence from its cause. Considered in itself it may fail to exist; through its cause it exists. Yet it is neither a body nor made of matter. This is no counterexample. Strictly speaking, a separate intellect has no essence distinct from its existence. Even on the common view that it has an essence, its receiving existence is not an external addition to a subject that already exists. It is not such an addition anywhere, least of all in an intellect.

    Moreover, the intellect's capacity is only the possibility of its existing; it is not a material readiness to receive something. If God, whose reality is sheer existence, had such a receptive capacity, it would have to be a material capacity carried by matter; matter in turn requires a form. God would then be bodily. He is far above that. — س قده

    ↩

  352. “Universal” here means comprehensive and encompassing, not an abstract general idea that leaves out individuals. A single higher form can contain a whole kind and its individuals, as a species-form or a complete whole encompasses what falls under it. — س قده

  353. The forms are not successive ideas that God thinks one after another. Their order is one of cause and effect, not time. — س قده

  354. Avicenna considers whether the forms exist in God, in separate Forms, or in another intellect or soul. Each option raises the question of how God knows the forms themselves.

  355. These beings are assumed to be free from matter. So placing them in the “divine realm” plainly cannot mean that they are parts of God's being or qualities added to it.

    It means that they take on qualities reflecting God's qualities, while the limitations that belong to possible beings become absorbed under the higher rules of necessary existence. Matter, movement, and their consequences are what make a thing seem separate from others. These beings are free from those conditions.

    That is why the author often says that the intellects endure through God's enduring existence and are without beginning through His beginninglessness. This does not contradict the spiritual teachers' claim that nothing besides God is without beginning, since the intellects do not possess an independent eternity.

    If that is how we speak of the intellects, which are God's acts, consider how much closer His own qualities must be. A quality is more closely joined to what it qualifies than an act is to its source, even when the act is one of creation without matter. There is therefore no basis for the complaint that no one knows what Avicenna means by the divine realm.

  356. If the forms exist in another intellect or soul, that being and its forms are effects of God. God must know that source and what proceeds from it. If that knowledge differs from the forms' existence, another form is needed to know them, and the chain begins again.

  357. At first it might seem that Avicenna's argument must concern the thing itself: its knowledge of itself would have to come before it, so that we could say the thing was known and then came to exist. Its form would then be in some other intellect or soul, and the same question would arise again without end.

    If the argument concerned only representations impressed upon an intellect, it might look equally damaging to Avicenna and to the view that the forms are present in God's own being. But on closer inspection, Avicenna's point is stronger. The forms under discussion would be things that exist in their own right. Their existence would therefore have to be preceded by knowledge. They would not themselves be merely known forms able to dispense with another act of knowledge.

    Forms impressed upon God's being in the rival account are, by contrast, already forms of knowledge rather than separately existing things. Avicenna has treated the separate forms and their place in the same way. His objection resembles the one the author raised earlier against those who accept separate Platonic forms.

    — س قده

    ↩

  358. The chain would either circle back on itself or continue without end. Both are impossible.

    ↩

  359. By “relation” the author means a relation as one of the categories we use in thought, and by “cause” he means causation considered through such a relation. He is speaking about the condition that comes with the relation, not the true relation in which being is given or the real, dependent causation through which existence flows. God's existence is necessary in every respect.

    A relation considered merely as a category is a concept drawn by the mind. It is plainly different from, and dependent on, the reality of the thing to which we apply it. We cannot treat such a concept as necessary in itself. Yet it may still truly describe a thing under one of its aspects. The aspect through which something is known is that very thing viewed in a weaker way. This is like calling a person “a father” or “a universal kind”: the description adds something to our way of thinking, not a new part to the person's existence. That is the sense in which relational attributes can be said to be “additional.”

    The passage also accepts the philosophers' language of intelligible forms as following from the divine essence, and answers an objection: would that not join possible things to God? Properly speaking, what is possible here is only the relational idea of God being a knower. The forms themselves are necessary through the necessity of the divine essence, eternal through its eternity, and enduring through its endurance. This is an even stronger claim than the statement that the First Intellect endures through God, rather than through some separate act that keeps it alive.

    ↩

  360. The causal order applies to the chain of separate intellects, not to Plato's “horizontal” Forms. The note suggests that Plato's Forms might still reflect, in a secondary way, the order of higher realities. — س قده

    ↩

  361. Avicenna distinguishes between a form that could be understood and a form that exists as already intelligible. The forms from God belong to the second kind.

  362. “Agency” can mean either the relation that exists after maker and made exist, or the source that brings about the effect. God's real agency is the latter and does not depend on the effect's prior existence.

  363. By “renewed reception,” the author means that a thing must receive a change from something other than itself. If a feature followed from a thing simply because of what the thing is, it would not be a new reception of this kind.

    By “through readiness,” he means that matter must take part, because matter carries powers that can become actual. Water receiving heat is a renewed change that depends on readiness. But the number four's being even is not a change that it receives in this way; nor is fire's being hot in the same sense. These features do not come from another thing acting through some material base. Even if we imagined four and fire apart from matter, their natures would still require those features. In such cases, saying that the feature “belongs to” the thing and saying that it “follows from” its nature amount to the same thing.

  364. Bahmanyār's word “subject” can mean simply that the forms depend on God. It need not mean that God receives them as a changing subject receives an accident. — س قده

  365. The author's point is that knowing God's essence and knowing what necessarily follows from it are not two events. The existence of the forms is bound up with God's knowledge of them.

  366. Suhrawardī is considering several possible orders: the forms may come before their effects, after them, or together with them. The author says each option seems to create a problem unless one sees that knowing and existence are the same here. — س قده

  367. Suhrawardī's argument would make God's essence, by itself, insufficient to produce external effects. The author accepts that forms are involved, but denies that this invalidates the account of the first intellect.

  368. The first intellect can be established by several arguments, not only by the claim that one simple cause produces one effect. — س قده

  369. A plurality of aspects does not license arbitrary effects. Each form is the source of what corresponds to it in the proper order. — س قده

  372. Suppose a feature necessarily belongs to something and comes from that thing's own reality, not from an outside source. Since the source gives rise to the feature, it cannot lack the perfection that it gives. The feature must therefore be present in the source's own reality, though it need not be present in the same limited way. The forms that belong to God's knowledge come from His very being. They are present in Him in a higher and more complete way. If their higher, unified level belongs necessarily to Him, how could that level involve either a possibility of not existing or a capacity waiting to be realized? Even at their lower, more distinct level, these forms have no independent standing beside Him.

    The intellects brought into being by God have forms belonging to His knowledge, but in relation to Him they are like words whose meaning depends on something else. They exist through God's existence and endure through His enduring reality. If even these created intellects have no independent being alongside Him, this is still more true of the forms that belong to His eternal attributes.

  373. The objection says one form would cause both the first effect and another form. A similar question arises for the first intellect, which causes both a second intellect and the outermost sphere. — س قده

  374. The forms follow from God's complete essence; they are not additions that make Him more complete. Their existence is an effect of His perfection, not a perfection He receives.

  375. If even separate effects do not make God more complete, the same is even more true of forms that are inseparable from His essence. — س قده

    ↩

  376. Avicenna's question concerns whether the forms' existence makes God know them, or whether God's knowing them makes them exist. The second is the right account, because the forms come from His knowledge. — س قده

    ↩

  377. God's self-knowledge is not caused by the forms. It is identical with His essence and is already complete. — س قده

  378. If the forms' existence caused God's knowledge and God's knowledge caused their existence, each would cause itself. The author says their existence and being known are one reality. — س قده

  379. The argument continues the same point: if knowing and existence were separate, either would need to come first and cause the other. — س قده

  380. God does not learn about things from the things themselves. He gives them existence, and knows them as effects that proceed from Him. — س قده

Avicenna considers three readings of the claim that God knows things before they exist: He knows them while wholly nonexistent; He knows them when they exist, by receiving knowledge from them; or He knows them through prior forms. The first makes a nonexistent thing knowable, the second makes God receptive to change, and the third risks an endless chain of forms.

  383. Descriptions based on relations or negation do not add a real perfection to God. The problem would arise only if an independent positive quality were added to His essence. — س قده

  384. The main issue is not whether God can be called the “subject” of something in a loose sense. It is whether the divine essence contains a real multiplicity. — س قده

  389. The author means that a simple source may be both the source and the basis of what follows from it, without being divided into a giver and a receiver.

  390. A human soul begins as an intellect in potential and receives forms over time. A being that is always fully actual has no such receptive stage; the very forms that follow from it may be both caused and present in it.

  391. If this statement comes from someone who holds, like the author, that God's utterly simple reality contains all existence in a higher way, its meaning is this: God's greatness lies in knowing Himself, and in that same knowledge knowing everything else. His knowledge gathers all things into one without losing their distinct details.

    Those who explain divine knowledge through separate forms usually accept a simpler and more general knowledge in God's essence. The forms do not add perfection to Him. Rather, they proceed from His essence, which already possesses perfection at a higher level.

    If the statement comes from someone who does not accept the author's full view, it has another sense. God's greatness does not depend on knowing forms or external things merely as objects outside Him. It lies in His bringing things forth as intelligible realities, considered in their relation to Him as lights and knowledge. In that respect they depend entirely on Him; His perfection does not come from something other than Himself.

    An objection may be raised: do not all these thinkers already agree that God's simple essence contains knowledge of everything? Why present this view as the special insight of only a few? The reply is that a conclusion may follow from someone's teaching without that thinker ever noticing it—or even being willing to accept it if it were pointed out. The same implication might be drawn from ordinary statements that God is self-sufficient and knows Himself and others. But explicitly recognising and proving that His single knowledge is detailed, not merely general, is a further claim. The author therefore treats it as a discovery shared with a few earlier masters of philosophy.

    ↩

  392. “Receive,” “be completed by,” and “be described by” can each suggest a different problem: change over time, dependence on another, or added qualities. None applies to forms that arise from God's essence without making Him more complete. — س قده

  393. Avicenna's followers do not all explain the point in the same way as the author. The forms are not divine perfections because of their meanings as concepts; they are God's detailed knowledge insofar as they arise from His own essence, without an outside cause or receiver.

  394. The author reads Avicenna to mean that God's knowledge of Himself entails the existence of these forms. Since His self-knowledge is direct, it is also the source of their existence. — س قده

    ↩

  395. “An existence that can be understood” means an existence that has the capacity to be known. A separate intellect, by contrast, exists in a way that is already intelligible. — س قده

    ↩

  396. The relation is purely intellectual and dependent, not a physical relation between a form and matter or an accident and its subject. — س قده

    ↩

  397. If the forms exist from God through the same simple act by which He knows them, then they are not separate from Him in existence. This suggests a kind of union between knower and known, though the author says its exact nature is hard to grasp.

  398. The sentence means that God is both knower and known because He knows Himself as the source of all things.

  399. The fact that many forms come after God's essence and stand in an order of cause and effect does not remove the difficulty. The objection made by Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī concerns the claim that forms are qualities present in God's being, as some philosophers say when they describe them as imprinted in Him or as inseparable features joined to Him. Even if those forms make up an ordered series, if they dwell in God's being, then His being is the place in which many distinct things exist. If they do not dwell in Him but stand apart and come from Him, the account begins to resemble the separate Forms that these philosophers reject.

    Those Forms, moreover, do not stand in a causal chain; thinkers of the Illuminationist school place them side by side. An ordered series of forms would not, by itself, require two separate principles in God, one to bring them forth and another to receive them, provided the necessity of the forms came from His very being and not from an outside source. But that does not resolve the main objection. The created intellects and lower things do not divide God's reality precisely because they exist in themselves, not in Him. If they were placed in Him, He would become the bearer of many things. Nor can we say that an ordered series is not really many.

    Differences between higher and lower causes remain differences; the cause and what it causes cannot be simply the same thing.

  400. God knows Himself, and knowing a cause includes knowing what follows from it. So He knows the whole. As the Qur'an asks, “Does He who created not know?” That is: does the Creator and cause of all else not know what He created? He is subtle and fully aware. He is free from matter; and, in the argument used here, every being free from matter knows itself. Knowledge of the cause therefore brings knowledge of the effect.

    When al-Fārābī says that there is no multiplicity in God, he may mean His knowledge of all things in one complete act. That follows because a reality wholly without parts contains everything in a simple way, without separate pieces. Differences remain only between the meanings of the divine names and what follows from them, which are the natures of things. If instead he means God's detailed knowledge that follows this complete knowledge, as in al-Fārābī's own account, the many objects of that knowledge are understood in their proper order, as the author explains.

    — س قده

  401. God's knowledge of all things is implicit in His self-knowledge; His detailed knowledge of them follows from knowing Himself as their cause. — س قده

    ↩

  402. If divine knowledge is described as detailed, saying that knowledge of all things comes 'after' knowledge of God's essence is easy enough to understand as an order of explanation. If divine knowledge is one and undivided, 'after' must mean something else. We first establish God's essence and His knowledge of Himself, then use these to establish His knowledge of all things. Or, in thought, we first consider His essence, then His being knowing, then His knowing other things. None of these stages is a change in God.

    We find a similar order when reports speak of God knowing, willing, intending, measuring, decreeing, and bringing about. Mystical writers likewise speak first of the divine essence without distinction, and then of names and attributes. The order belongs to explanation, not to God's life in time.

    In the sentence under discussion, 'after His essence' describes all the things whose existence is subsequent to His, rather than serving as a claim about when His knowledge occurs. The statement says that His knowledge of those things, like His knowledge of Himself, is His very essence. Some copies of the Fusus omit the words 'His very essence.'

    The statement that 'all things are united in relation to His essence' can be read through either simple or detailed divine knowledge. It is especially plain on the first reading. On the second, the author's account of the order of causes shows how many things are related through one source.

    The better reading is that the Teacher is explaining why an infinite range of different things does not introduce multiplicity into God's essence or His knowledge. God's one, simple existence discloses things that are many and unlike one another, because they all depend on that one stable source. Their shared dependence joins what is otherwise scattered and brings what differs into relation.

    The expression 'He is all things in unity' seems to point to the principle that simple reality contains everything in a higher way. Someone might instead say that 'all things' here means the created world as one whole, since God's essence simply knows that whole. But this reading is strained, and it gives the pronouns in the passage different references. — س قده

    ↩

  403. The critic's claim that the First Effect is “in” God would prove something only if “in” meant that it inheres in Him as an accident. That is precisely what the author denies.

    ↩

  404. Avicenna argues that the forms exist through God's knowing them, and God's knowing them is not a second act added to that existence. If one were distinct from the other, the same circular dependence or endless chain would return.

    ↩

  405. This is not like the relation of physical things to God. Bodies remain because He preserves them and exist because He creates them. Their dependence is plain: matter and its features, including change, time, and place, reveal how limited and distinct they are. In the separate intellects, even these signs of limitation are almost lost. Their relation to God is closer still, although they are among His acts, not His attributes.

    The author has been challenged for speaking this way about the intellects. If their everlasting existence belongs to God's own everlasting existence, the critic argues, then their being would be His being, and His being theirs. One of the author's contemporaries, Shams al-Gīlānī, quotes his discussion in The Treatise on Coming into Being and objects that a being possible in itself would then become necessary in itself.

    This objection looks more like a discussion of ordinary words than a careful philosophical distinction. Those who follow the approach sometimes called the taste of divine unity hold that possible essences exist through their relation to the self-subsisting Reality. Since the relation does not exist independently, in reality everything that exists does so through God's existence. Their teachers explain this in works such as Al-Taqdīsāt. Some even say that Zayd's existence is Zayd's God. Yet they do not conclude that a possible essence has become a necessary essence. On their view, the essence remains possible, while the existence through which it is present is another matter. That is why they speak of multiplicity among existing things and unity in existence itself.

    Perhaps the critic also objects to the spiritual teachers' claim that the meanings of the divine names and attributes exist through the One they name, so that a name is the same as the named Reality in one respect and different in another.

    Here, likewise, the intellects have essences to which possibility belongs, while their existence comes from God. Essence and existence must not be confused. Each has its own proper account.

    Even if we adopt the author's own position, according to which existence is fundamental and has levels differing in strength, the separate intellects still have no independent existence beside His. Their existence is dependent, like the meaning of a word that cannot stand alone but needs another word to complete it. One line of poetry says of such realities, “We were exalted letters that had not yet been spoken.” They show or point toward the divine essence. When something is considered only as a way of pointing to another, it has no independent standing. That is the meaning of saying the intellects belong to the divine domain and exist through God. In one respect they are not God; in another they are not entirely other than Him. The same applies to one who loses separate self-awareness in the reality contemplated.

    How, I wonder, can critics accept the saying attributed to ʿAlī, the foremost of those who ascend through knowledge, “I tore off the gate of Khaybar through divine strength,” while denying this relation? And how can they accept the Qur'anic words, “You did not throw when you threw, but God threw”? — S. R.

    — س قده

  406. Why does the argument speak specifically of what is first brought into being, when the same account also applies to things that are formed within the world? One answer is that the universal kinds found here are preserved as one individual succeeds another. Knowledge of particular things is then contained within knowledge of their universal kinds, as the philosophers in Aristotle’s school maintain. Another answer is that the whole of the world, considered without dividing it into separate things and in relation to the one God, is one thing issuing from the One. Scripture says, ‘Our command is but one.’ From this point of view, the whole is brought into being at once, without any prior matter or stretch of time.

    Matter, time, and place already belong to the whole we are considering; they cannot stand outside it as conditions for its creation. The argument is stated in universal terms because science deals with general statements. Compare ‘Every Necessary Being is simple’ or ‘For every Necessary Being, what it is and that it is are one.’ ‘Form’ can mean either what makes something actually exist or the form grasped by the intellect. — س قده

  407. One may object: how can the forms be without limit? The kinds of immaterial and material beings, whether heavenly or earthly, seem finite. Nor does this account assign a separate form in God to every one of infinitely many individuals. Further, if infinitely many forms are ordered as causes and effects, there seems to be an endless chain of causes bounded at either end.

    There are several replies to the first objection. “Without limit” may describe their range or intensity by reference to God's unlimited light, rather than an independent infinity of forms. That is why the author says that they are eternal through His eternity. Or the basic kinds of substances and qualities may be finite while their combinations are beyond counting. There are only a few basic tastes, for example, yet their mixtures have innumerable varieties. A further possibility is that the forms of particular things exist in God, each with the features that make it a kind represented by only one individual.

    The second objection assumes that the entire limitless collection forms one chain of causes. It need not. On the view that forms exist independently as dominating lights, the causal order belongs to the higher lights, not to the equal-ranking forms called exemplars. Moreover, the order extends towards the effects; it does not require an endless series leading upwards towards the first cause. — س قده

  410. These philosophers accept that God's perfect, all-embracing knowledge is identical with His essence and comes before particular things. That knowledge is enough when the things known are themselves forms whose very existence is detailed knowledge of them. God's giving them existence is then the same relation as His knowing them.

    But they say that external material things are different. For them, the simple knowledge in God's essence is not enough to explain His detailed knowledge of things outside Him. The forms must therefore proceed from Him before those external things come to exist. The objection cannot be forced on the philosophers of illumination, since they hold that God's producing external things and His knowing them are one relation. The Aristotle’s followers disagree, relying on their rule that what is directly known must exist for the knower, not merely in matter.

    A clearer way to put their argument may be this: God's existence is pure oneness and simplicity, while the many things outside Him are, by comparison, pure multiplicity. To connect the two, they posit an intermediate level that joins unity and multiplicity. This is the level of forms impressed in knowledge. The author's words can be understood in that sense. — س قده

  415. This passage has two purposes. First, someone might say that al-Khafrī only meant that God's knowledge of external things through forms is not perfect knowledge belonging to His essence. The reply is that God's knowledge of the forms is the very knowledge through which He knows the external things. In much the same way, knowing an image of the sun is a way of knowing the sun itself: the image is how we direct our attention to what it represents. We can distinguish what is known directly from what is known through it, but that does not give us two separate acts of knowledge or prove that one act comes after the other.

Their necessary connection with God concerns what they are, as existing qualities whose existence depends on the Necessary Being.   420. The First Being cannot be present in a mind as a mental image. He is pure reality, not something that can enter any mind and become an idea. Nor do the consequences that necessarily follow from Him need Him to be an object inside our thought. On the argument being discussed, they must therefore be real things rather than merely mental things.

    But this reasoning can be challenged by our own mental forms. Suppose the forms in our minds were properties of essences simply as essences. They would have to belong to those essences whether or not anything existed—an obviously false result. Suppose instead that they were “mental properties.” Would our souls then have to exist inside another mind before those properties could belong to them? That is also absurd. The argument would leave only the claim that our mental images are external properties, which contradicts what it set out to prove.

    The answer is that all these forms are real in themselves, because they belong to a soul that exists in reality. A feature of a real being is itself real. We call them “mental” only in comparison with the other real beings they represent. In the case of God, philosophers use “mental” for forms said to be present in divine knowledge, and “external” for beings that have their own standing or are present in matter, where one thing is absent from another. Indeed, by the usual test of whether something produces effects, the forms in divine knowledge would have a stronger claim to be called real: they are understood as sources of the things that appear in the world. — س قده

  421. One defence of the rule says that knowing a cause directly must bring with it direct knowledge of the effect. On that reading, the rule supports the view that God's knowledge is detailed and immediately present even while it is one complete act. It would not support the view held by Aristotle’s followers that He knows things through separate representations.

    But there is a difficulty with that reading. The rule was discussed by the philosophers in Aristotle’s school in the part of logic concerned with demonstration. They did not generally accept direct knowledge except in the case of a thing knowing itself. Moreover, demonstration works through ideas and judgments, not through immediate presence. If the rule applied only to direct awareness, the logical distinction between proofs that move from cause to effect and proofs that move from effect to cause would lose its purpose.

    Avicenna and other Aristotle’s followers therefore do not grant that a cause's knowledge of its effect, or an effect's knowledge of its cause, must be immediate awareness. Nor do they take this rule to establish that claim.

    — ط مد ظله

  422. Direct knowledge of another thing can come through union with it or through being its cause and encompassing it in existence. The author's claim is that God's knowledge of created existences works in this second way. — س قده

  423. One might object that, even if existence itself is what God brings into being, the rule that knowledge of a cause brings knowledge of its effects establishes only that He knows those effects somehow. Why must His knowledge be direct rather than through representations?

    The answer is that existence has no single fixed manner of being and no essence that could be represented by a separate image. An image represents the nature of an existing thing, not existence itself. To know a particular existence as such is therefore to know it by its presence. The author's point is that the rule used by everyone to establish that God knows other things also establishes how He knows them: directly, not through forms impressed upon a knower, as some thinkers maintain.

    A second objection follows. Earlier, the author seemed to criticize Suhrawardi, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, and others who regard existing things themselves as God's knowledge. He suggested that they had overlooked a familiar principle: for something directly perceived, its existence in itself and its existence as perceived are one. Material existence, however, is normally concealed from perception, while knowledge requires presence and disclosure. Why does he now seem to endorse the view he earlier challenged?

    In the earlier passage, he was explaining why the philosophers who rely on mental forms had adopted their position. Their rule made it difficult to call material things directly present to God. The thinkers who defended direct knowledge might not have accepted that rule, or they might have held that material things are not hidden from God. His knowledge embraces matter as well as everything else. Things with position and direction remain what they are, but before Him they are all equally present, as though gathered into a point.

    Here the author's task is different. He uses the established rule about knowing effects through their cause to reject knowledge by impressed forms and to support knowledge through presence. The main purpose is to challenge the theory of representations, not simply to repeat an earlier proof. — س قده

    But the heart of al-Tusi's argument is sound: if two causes are one, their immediate effects must also be one. Otherwise, many things would come directly from one source. In this case, there would be the forms arising from God's knowledge of Himself, which is identical with His being, and then the things corresponding to those forms, arising from His being again.

    Perhaps the author took al-Tusi to be arguing merely from a likeness between cause and effect: because the causes are one, it would be fitting for the effects to be one as well. That is not the force of the argument.

  430. If the divine forms were not connected to God's knowledge, one might treat them as separate realities existing on their own. But that would not make them ghostly images or bodies occupying places outside our world. They could instead be the inward realities of this world, not another set of objects beside it. Nor would that alone require infinitely many worlds.

    One interpretation of the Platonic Forms, discussed in the First Journey, treats them as independently existing measurable images, one for each particular member of each kind. The Teacher's point is that the divine forms should be understood as forms of knowledge, not as extended figures. If they were figures belonging to matter, they would be bodies, and bodies need places. This would put other bodily worlds alongside ours. Aristotle objected to such worlds, among other reasons because of the empty spaces they would require, as in the problem of two spheres touching at a single point.

    An endless series would follow as well. Each bodily world would have to be preceded by knowledge of it. But if that knowledge were itself a collection of separate, measurable bodies, it would make another world in need of yet earlier knowledge. There would be no end.

    There is another possible reading. Suppose the divine forms were not intellects and forms of knowledge belonging to the divine realm, standing inwardly and above this world. Suppose instead that they were separate intellects occupying a place outside it, alongside it, while the natural kinds here were not their shadows or effects. Such intellects would still act and produce natural forms. Just as things in this lower world reflect higher realities, these supposed intellects would produce lower worlds. Since these forms would themselves constitute a possible world, that world too would need earlier forms of knowledge, and so on without end.

    The issue is not that each divine form must be a whole world and that there are infinitely many forms. Rather, each world of forms is supposed to be preceded by another such world. On this reading, calling the forms 'images' means that they disclose the things beneath them. Describing them as being in places outside the world is a way of saying that they stand alongside it rather than above it in the order of causes. The first reading, however, seems the clearer one.

  434. If they understood that this oneness is true unity, not the numerical unity of one thing set against another, they would see the point. Every thing has a face turned toward God and a face turned toward itself. These two faces are not combined as one independent thing is combined with another, but more as an object is related to its shadow. A Persian verse says, in effect: “You are a radiant sun, and I am the shadow it casts in the west; the shadow's coming and going depend on the sun.” When the sun of truth rises, the passing appearances fade and all faces bow before the Living, the Sustainer.

    We have already established, in discussing existence and essence, that a thing's existence is simply the reality of that thing. Its essence does not become real in any other way. Consider blackness. As a meaning, it is blackness; as something real, it exists. But the actual occurrence of blackness is not a second thing added to a blackness that already existed. What was supposedly awaiting this addition would itself have no determinate reality. The actual blackness is one instance of existence. Reality deserves the name “real” more fully than anything that becomes real only through it.

    The difference, then, is between qualities within one reality, not a separation between two independent things. As the Qur'an says of invented gods, “They are only names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority.” The objection that prompted these remarks may therefore be met by distinguishing a thing's true existence from the names and descriptions we attach to it. — س قده

  444. This is a mistake. What exists only potentially is the detailed knowledge of answers when those answers depend on the imagination. If their images are not in the imagination, we may wrongly suppose the answers are absent from the intellect. And because the answers are not there as a number of separate details, we may suppose they are not there in a single, gathered form either.

    But the simple knowledge that has become a settled ability is already knowledge. Indeed, it is actual: the person does not need to acquire the subject again before answering. What is still potential is the display of that knowledge as separate, numerous answers—not its possession as a unified and powerful understanding.

    One can go further, although thinkers of this school may resist it. Knowledge may be more distinct and exact in that unified state. Distinctness follows existence, which is itself the power to appear and be known. The fuller an existence is, the more perfectly it can contain distinctions, even when these are not spread out in time. Different ideas appropriate to the settled understanding can be drawn from it. That understanding is stronger in existence than the changing images in the imagination. It creates and supplies those images. Because it produces them, the original writer may have mistaken it for a mere power to know rather than knowledge itself.

    The point is that even the second kind of human knowledge—the settled ability that a person cannot yet draw on because the needed conditions are absent—is actual knowledge. So are having it in the imagination and possessing it in the intellect, and knowing things as a number of separate details and knowing them together as one. The soul is not exhausted by its imagination, not even in its highest capacity. An object can therefore be absent from imagination without being absent from the soul's simple understanding. — س قده

  466. Every being free from matter is capable of understanding and can itself be understood. There is no barrier between such beings. Each therefore knows the others, whether they are above it, below it, or at the same level.

    This explains the statement that intellectual beings receive forms of things that are not their own effects. The point is not that God knows some things directly and others by receiving images of them. God knows both these beings and the forms within them through their presence to Him. Nor does it mean that an intellect knows its own effects merely through representations. The intended distinction concerns things that are not its effects.

    Such things include higher intellects that cause a lower intellect to exist, and intellects at the same level, neither of which causes the other. They also include, for each governing intellect, the material forms governed by other intellects. Each material form depends on the higher being responsible for it, not on the being responsible for a different form.

    Why does an intellect know these other beings? Nothing separate from matter is hidden from another such being. Moreover, every intellect knows the Necessary Being, and everything else is His effect. Knowledge of a cause entails knowledge of its effects. All created things must therefore be knowable to every separate intellect, whether they are above it or below it. What lies below it as its own effect is known directly through presence.

    Why are forms needed for things it does not cause? When the thing known is neither identical with the knower nor subject to it as an effect, its form must be brought before the knower. Thus an intellect knows higher intellects and those alongside it through forms, since it does not govern them.

    God, however, knows everything directly. Every being is either His immediate effect or the effect of one of His effects. The condition for direct knowledge of another—the complete power by which it is made present—is fulfilled in His case for all beings. He knows Himself as the cause of the first effect and thereby knows that effect. The first effect causes the second, which is also known directly through its cause, and the same applies throughout the order of existence. Similarly, each separate intellect directly knows what lies beneath it as its own effect, through its power to illuminate and govern it. The higher principles therefore know directly even the bodies that depend on them, all the more so the First Principle of all principles.

Suppose the objection means that God, or any immaterial being, directly perceives particular material things, and calls that perception “sensation.” We can accept the implication and deny that it is absurd. Those who say that God's knowledge is a kind of sight do not shrink from this conclusion. Thinkers who say that God hears and sees but needs no bodily organs—including the author—must mean that every existent is directly present to Him. Visible, audible, and other particular things are among those existents. He therefore sees and hears them directly, not merely by knowing general descriptions of them.

    For us, particular things become present through bodily senses because we need them. For God, they are present through His own essence. As the reports put it, His whole being is hearing and His whole being is sight.

    But if the objection uses “sensation” to mean a bodily faculty housed in an organ, the implication fails. Direct perception of particulars is not the same as possessing a material sense-organ. “Perception” can sometimes be contrasted with abstract understanding or knowledge. The difficult case here is the material particular, which has position, extension, and quantity. An immaterial particular presents no comparable problem: understanding a separate intellect or an immaterial particular is an act of intellect. That is why it is said that every immaterial being knows itself.

  490. At first sight, it is difficult to say that a distinguishing feature or a form is itself a kind of existence. Existence has no broader kind, no defining feature, and nothing corresponding to them. Also, saying that something is a kind of existence does not, by itself, mean it lacks an essence. Whiteness, for example, is a kind of being, but we can still say what whiteness is.

    Consider the real features from which definitions are drawn. A body's bodily form corresponds to its capacity to have three dimensions. The plant soul corresponds to growing. The sensing and moving soul corresponds to sensation and movement by choice. Surely each of these has a nature we can describe. Otherwise nothing would have an essence at all.

    The answer is that the author is speaking particularly about the defining perfections of substances such as rational souls and separate intellects. Following the Illuminationist philosopher, he often says that human souls and intellects are pure lights, or pure existences, without a separate limited essence. An essence, in this account, is a concept that describes an existence confined within limits. Intellects are not confined in that way; souls, too, do not remain fixed within a single limit.

    A little later he will deny that the kinds of animal life below humanity possess distinct, positive defining perfections of this sort. The differences used in their definitions are ways in which their more general nature grows stronger. These differences are not separate existences added to the animal, but they are not mere absences either: an absence could not help make something the kind of thing it is. The final positive perfection, on this account, is the human being's holy or rational soul, a way of existing rather than an additional essence.

  492. Otherwise the human being could not be the last and most complete kind, gathering the earlier kinds within it. Or it would have to be put together from features that stand alongside one another rather than forming an ordered whole. There is a distinction here between considering the human being and a horse as separate kinds, and considering how lower forms are gathered into higher ones. When we consider the earlier forms as distinct things, they are like matter in relation to the last form. When we consider what they share without separating them from what completes them, they are wider kinds, and the final distinguishing feature gives them their completed identity.

    This is one meaning of the saying, ‘The greater world is folded within you.’ Someone might object: how could a wider kind exist without its distinguishing feature, or matter without form, when the feature or form is what makes it complete? The reply is that denying a particular feature does not deny the more general reality. In the final kind, its last distinguishing feature completes all the wider kinds, and its last form completes all earlier material levels. This fits especially well with the view that the soul changes in its very existence until it becomes united with the active intellect. That intellect, by God's permission, brings natural kinds to their completion and gathers what is actual in them, just as prime matter gathers their possibilities.

    A simpler way of stating the point is that animal life may count as a complete kind among animals but, in the human being, is included within a fuller reality.

  493. God is the source who gives existence to all beings directly, and through their existence gives rise to all the different kinds of things. One principle therefore requires that every form of existence be present in Him in a higher, simpler, and more complete way. Other principles require that He be the source of every meaning and concept, without those meanings existing within Him as separate, limited things.

    His knowledge of His own complete existence is thus the very same as His knowledge of all existences and all kinds. Because His existence is one and simple, that knowledge is also one. Yet it reveals all things distinctly. Existence is light, and the stronger that light becomes, the more clearly things can be disclosed. If different meanings are distinguishable through the weak, scattered lights of the world, they can be disclosed still more clearly in the single, powerful light of the eternal source. Their unity there does not erase their differences.

    That explanation follows the author's own principles. The explanation favored by some mystics instead says that God pours out the kinds of things through His names and the forms of those names. In that account their fixed realities are present in the divine names. As they put it, glory belongs to the One who joins unity to unity and multiplicity to multiplicity. That approach will be discussed later.

    An objection: this may explain God's direct and complete knowledge of things eternally, before they appear. But how can He already know them as actual effects, since they come into existence in time?

    The answer is that the existence spread through things is the appearance of one reality in many forms. The earlier account described many things contained in one source; this describes one source appearing through many things. These two levels are not separate realities. Created existence depends on its source like a word whose meaning depends on its connection to other words. It cannot stand alone, and whatever is true of it is grounded in that source. Seen as a whole, the existence spread through many things is still one light, while also disclosing each thing in detail. It belongs to the divine order and is prior to created things by the priority of its source, not by being an earlier event in time.

    Furthermore, the kinds present in divine knowledge are the very kinds that appear in the world. Their existence in knowledge is complete in a way that embraces the limited forms they later have. To grasp the complete reality is to grasp what appears from it. Once we understand how cause and effect belong together, the difficulty falls away.

    The question of divine knowledge is central to theology. Many other questions can be understood through it, especially the unity of God. The claim that the one, simple reality includes all beings in a higher way is, at heart, a claim about direct divine knowledge. — س قده

    Second, why would God's knowledge of things need these intellects to carry the forms of other things, like books containing His knowledge? That question, too, is not the present one. The answer belongs to the account of the levels of knowledge. Because these intellects are actually immaterial, their knowledge is their very existence, even if it is not identical with what they are. An immaterial being knows itself and the things that come from it. The knowledge of one such being does not make the knowledge of another unnecessary. Each also counts as God's knowledge at the level of His acts, because its reality and what it knows are present to Him.

If God's own essence is already simple knowledge of all things, and if that one knowledge is detailed as well as simple, what need is there for forms alongside Him or for separate Platonic forms and lights? The author has already said that those who place God's detailed knowledge after His essence have not understood the point. Why, then, must these additional forms themselves be detailed knowledge? The following argument is meant to answer this third question. — س قده

  499. The word here is a verbal noun linked to its object. An objection may be raised: knowing a cause must involve knowing its effects, but why must that knowledge take the form of separate images? If knowledge of the effects is already contained in knowledge of the cause itself, the principle is satisfied even more fully. So the question remains.

    The reply lies in the author's words, “in the way in which it is its effect.” Knowing the cause means knowing each effect in its higher mode of existence, where it is present in its divine source. But it also means knowing that effect in its own mode of existence, as the actual effect that follows from the cause. On the account being discussed, this second kind of knowledge is through forms.

    There is another objection. If these forms exist together with the knower, we can see how knowledge is through forms. But what if they exist separately as intelligences made of light? On the Platonic account, they are themselves acts of knowing. The reply is that, although they are knowledge in themselves, they are also independent forms through which material things are known. Seen in relation to God, they are His lights and His knowledge: they exist through Him and are eternal through His eternity. Seen as His effects in their own right, they are things known. The same realities can therefore be forms of knowledge in one respect and objects of knowledge in another. — س قده

  501. This passage explains more than the immediate question. It helps us understand the realm in which things were first known, divine decree and destiny, and the descent of spirits without their leaving their own higher level or changing their essential nature. It also explains how they can ascend without the higher level having changed.

    The essence of a thing remains recognisable through its different appearances, and its ways of existing have one continuing source. So when a natural being descends to the lower level that belongs to its kind of existence, that descent can be described as the descent of its higher, divine or intellectual reality. Yet the higher reality has not abandoned its own level. When the natural being rises, its rising is truly a return to its higher source, because it has never been cut off from that source. The higher reality and the lower reflection are one truth understood at different levels.

    The difficulty and the value of this knowledge lie in holding both sides together. Earth and matter have no place in the world beyond matter, yet what appears here is connected to that higher world and can rise toward the heavens and angels. Conversely, the world of bodies cannot contain a soul in its full reality, still less an intellect. Such beings have no bodily position or direction, yet their influence comes from their own source into this world, fills it, and gives it order. The Qur'an speaks of God ordering the affair from heaven to earth, “then it rises to Him.” The movement is real in the lower being, without requiring the higher source to change places. — س قده

  504. The passage about reaching the heavenly bodies might seem to say that individual souls, after passing through the levels of earthly bodies, attach themselves to one celestial sphere after another and finally unite with the universal Soul and universal Intellect. Some thinkers have understood the journey that way. But taken literally it would involve a soul passing from body to body, which is reincarnation. We should instead read the journey as a continuous rise in being: the soul develops and changes inwardly, through changes in its very existence.

    On one interpretation, the “heavenly body” is the subtle spirit associated with the brain. Because it is refined and balanced, it resembles a celestial sphere; it carries the soul's powers, serves as the camp of its forces, and receives life. Or the phrase may refer to the enduring body of the world of images.

    A better interpretation, in my view, is that the soul is attached to a heavenly body as something can appear through a visible form without becoming that form's soul. Suppose a person has an intense attachment to a beloved image and can encounter it only through a reflection in water or crystal. That does not make the person the soul of the water or crystal. Nor does the soul's reaching the universal Soul and universal Intellect mean it must literally inhabit each heavenly body in turn.

    Skipping all those heavenly levels would look like a sudden leap, unless the soul had already advanced so far during earthly life that it no longer needed a body at all. The prophets may travel in that way, and there may be others. But someone still attached to the forms, pleasures, and habits of this world cannot pass beyond them without loosening those bonds completely. Such a person must turn away from constant concern with eating, drinking, and the other habits of bodily life, and cease clinging to sights, sounds, and passing particulars. — س قده

  527. Divine decree is the all-embracing knowledge that follows the level of the divine essence. It has several forms. There is decree in a gathered state: the forms present in the Pen, meaning the First Intellect and, taken together, the ordered series of intellects. Their ordered connection makes them one whole. There is a first detailed decree: the forms present in the intellects considered separately, as a group on the same level. And there is a second detailed decree: the forms passed on to the universal souls through their intellectual side. These are also called the Preserved Tablet and the Mother of the Book. The term “Mother of the Book” can also refer to decree taken as a whole.

    Destiny likewise has two forms. One belongs to knowledge: the forms present in the celestial souls and in the world of images. The other belongs to things as they actually occur: the ordered stages in the record of existence itself. The author has set aside that last account in this book.

    Every kind of decree and destiny has a source from which it comes and something in which it is received. We must also distinguish a receiver we identify only by an act of thought from a receiver that exists in reality.

    The source of decree in its gathered state is divine care. Its receiver as considered in thought is the nature of the Pen. The forms are not, in the author's mature account, additional things lodged inside it. They are the fuller, simpler way in which the lower existences already exist in the Pen. They become distinguishable only when we think of the concepts and essences belonging to them, much as the fixed realities are linked to God's names. So the capacity attributed to the Pen in thought is also the capacity attributed to these forms. Their receiver in reality is the lower Tablets. On the different view of philosophers who picture forms as imprinted on a knowing subject, their real receiver is the subject in which the imprint occurs.

    The source of the first detailed decree is the Pen. Its receiver considered in thought is essence, while its real receiver is the Preserved Tablet—or, for those who accept imprinted forms, the subject that holds those forms. A similar account applies to the second detailed decree and to destiny. There is one important difference: the receiver of the forms of destiny is not merely identified by thought, because those forms are added to the things in which they appear. Thus the author's reference to the “places” of decree means both kinds of receiver—the Pen and the Preserved Tablet—while the real receiver of destiny is the Tablet of Erasure and Confirmation.

  533. “Destiny,” in this discussion, means the measure and arrangement of a thing, including the limits and particular features of its existence. In ordinary crafts we see how measurement works. A tailor measures cloth before cutting and sewing it. A carpenter measures wood to make a chair with a certain shape. A mould gives the material poured into it a particular size, form, and appearance.

    When we apply the idea to real existence, destiny refers to the particular qualities and effects that a thing receives from the causes involved in its coming into being. Each kind of cause, each condition, the place where it acts, and everything that prepares the way can affect the outcome. The surrounding factors also shape the thing's later properties and actions. Together they are like a mould determining how the finished object will be.

    Three conclusions follow. First, a predicted result may fail to occur if “destiny” is being considered in relation to only some of the causes. A partial cause does not guarantee what the complete set of causes would produce. Second, destiny in this particular sense belongs to the material world. Here there are many causes, and they support or obstruct one another. In a realm free of matter, the complete cause does not require matter, a bodily form, surrounding conditions, preparatory causes, or the removal of obstacles. Only the cause that acts and the purpose of its action remain; in a fully actual immaterial being these are united. Third, divine decree has a wider reach than destiny in this narrow sense. Decree applies beyond the material world as well.

    If we expand the word “destiny” to include every kind of limit, even the limits used to define a thing's essence, it can then apply to material and immaterial beings alike, just as decree does. Under that wider meaning it also does not fail to take effect. — ط مد ظله

  541. A dictionary explains “the splendours of God's face” as the lights of His face. In a commentary on The Philosophy of Illumination, the phrase means the lights of the eternal essence. When the angels nearest to God behold them, they glorify Him, overcome by His majesty and greatness.

    Why is the number seventy thousand used? One explanation begins with seven levels in the human being, the subtle faculties mentioned in the previous note. It adds the nine heavenly spheres and the one world of elements, making ten. Existence is of one kind, though its levels differ in how fully their effects appear. Just as the earthly soul has seven inner levels, so do the heavenly souls. Seven multiplied by ten gives seventy. Each level is a place where a thousand of God's beautiful names are displayed, making seventy thousand levels and veils. Their existence is a veil of light; our concepts of them can become veils of darkness.

    It may be clearer to reverse the calculation: each of the seven levels contains ten elements. In this symbolic account the human being is formed from ten portions—one from the elements and nine from the heavenly spheres. Pride is linked with the sphere of the sun, anger with Mars, love with Venus, and so on. Each of the seven levels contains these influences in its own way and reflects the divine names.

    Another explanation takes the lights to mean separate intellects and bodies. On that reading seventy thousand expresses an immense number, not an exact total. The intellects corresponding to the kinds of earthly, marine, heavenly, and stellar beings would be beyond counting. Or we may say that the intellectual world gathers the ten bodily worlds and their seven levels into a higher unity, each level disclosing the divine names. God knows best.

According to the report, God created a name that was not a spoken sound, a physical shape, a color, or anything that could be compared with a created thing. It was free of direction and limit, beyond the grasp of the senses and imagination. Though hidden, it was not covered by anything.

    God made it a complete word with four parts, none of which came before the others. He disclosed three parts because creatures needed them and kept one part hidden—the treasured name. He then assigned four supports to each of the three disclosed names, making twelve. For each support He made thirty names of action, making three hundred and sixty in all.

    The report gives examples of these names and qualities: the Merciful, the Compassionate, the King, the Holy, the Creator, the Maker, the Shaper, the Living, the Sustainer who does not sleep, the Knowing, the Aware, the Hearing, the Seeing, the Wise, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Supreme, the Most High, the Great, the Powerful, the Giver of Peace, the Giver of Faith, the Guardian, the Originator, the Incomparable, the Exalted, the Majestic, the Generous, the Provider, the Giver of Life, the Bringer of Death, the Resurrector, and the Inheritor. The list continues until the total reaches three hundred and sixty.

    They are called “seas” because of the abundance of existence and effects that flow from them. If there are three hundred and sixty active influences on the side of the source, there are corresponding ways of receiving those influences on the side of what is created. The comparison extends to the three hundred and sixty degrees of the heavenly sphere.

  547. The sphere's movement should not be compared to a ship moving one way while its passengers move the other. Circular motion can occur while something inside the sphere remains still. — س قده

  548. The speaker does not mean that Hell is literally contained within the celestial sphere. The point is that sense-perception reaches this limit. If a person sees the sphere and its contents as separate from God, rather than as signs of His names and attributes, they may approach the world of Hell. The seven gates of Hell are compared to the five outer senses and two inner senses, common sense and imagination. For those who rise toward God, the Footstool is a passage toward Paradise.

  549. When we attribute knowledge, power, life, and similar qualities to God, we begin with qualities that we recognize as perfections in beings like ourselves. We then remove everything in them that involves absence, limitation, or weakness. What remains is a pure perfection, which can be truly attributed to God. He is pure perfection, lacking nothing that counts as a perfection. The real difficulty is to understand power in this way, whichever of its two definitions we use. Human power, with all its bodily and limited features, cannot be attributed to Him unchanged.

    Consider the first definition: the ability either to act or not to act. Here ability means that neither alternative is ruled out by the nature of the agent. The agent is not forced into inaction because acting is impossible, nor forced into acting because inaction is impossible. In short, the agent is not bound by either alternative. The definition does not say that power must be different from the one who has it. Our power is something other than our essence, but that need not be so in every case.

    Proofs have already shown that God's existence contains no absence, that He is unlimited, and that He brings everything into being through His own essence, not through something added to Him from outside. Since His essence is the source of His action and is itself unrestricted, He cannot be confined either to acting because not acting is impossible, or to not acting because acting is impossible. His power is precisely this freedom from limitation, and it is identical with His essence.

    Nothing above Him or equal to Him can force an action upon Him; nothing else exists independently of Him in that way. Nor can one of His acts force Him to produce that act or another, since every act comes after Him in the order of dependence and relies on Him in every aspect of its existence. It would be especially absurd to suppose that God first gives His action the necessity by which it exists, and is then Himself compelled by that necessity to perform it. This shows how He acts freely under the first definition of power.

    Consider the second definition: an agent who acts if He wills and does not act if He does not will. This connects acting with will. In us, will is a state of the soul. It follows our knowledge of a benefit that moves us to act—or, put more simply, an additional motive. We act because that motive is present and we know it. Our capacity to act is therefore tied to our knowledge of something that gives us a reason to act.

    Now suppose we affirm will in God's essence, taking it to mean knowledge of what is best. We have already established that God acts through His very essence, and that His knowledge is identical with His essence. What limits human agency—our separately acquired will and knowledge—is therefore, in God, none other than His unrestricted essence. The second definition also applies: He acts through will and through knowledge of what is best, knowing the thing together with the good achieved through its existence. His power means that His essence is the source of every good and every benefit.

    But a benefit that follows an action in the outside world is not a goal that God needs to reach or a motive that makes Him act. Rather, that benefit is present in His knowledge, which is His essence. It would make no sense to say that God's knowledge depends on an external result. The goodness of an action follows from the action; the action, in turn, follows from God as its source. Its later benefit therefore cannot act back upon Him, control His action, or compel Him. Nothing else can compel Him either. He is free without qualification.

    Under both definitions, then, divine power means that the agent is unrestricted. No necessity imposed by the act or its omission limits Him. By contrast, if power is taken to mean that an act is entirely undecided because the agent provides no determining cause, that would deny genuine agency and leave the act to mere chance. — Ṭ. M.

  550. “Possible” can mean that supposing something to happen leads to no impossibility. This is possibility in practice, as distinct from possibility in itself. Consider the nonexistence of the First Intellect. Considered in its own nature, the First Intellect is a possible being: it does not exist necessarily through itself. But it is not possible, in the other sense, for it to fail to exist when its necessary source exists. To suppose its absence would lead to the impossible claim that God does not exist. God is far above that.

    If we understand God's freedom to act as possibility in itself, we meet the difficulty already mentioned. If we understand it as possibility in practice, the difficulty is greater. Some theologians have gone further still. Rather than saying that an act of creation could be interrupted, they say such interruptions actually occur across an imagined, endless series of times. On careful examination, all these claims are impossible.

  560. The discussion began with power, whereas Avicenna's words concern choice. The result is the same. Choosing an act means that it follows four principles: knowledge, intention, will, and power. Choice can be understood as the combination of these, rather than as one further thing.

    If a reason or motive guides the choice, then power acts through that motive too. In us, a motive is a branch of knowledge: it includes a judgment that doing the act will bring some benefit. And if intention and will both depend on that motive, the exercise of power must also depend on it, because they come before the exercise of power and intention is part of how power is defined.

    Intention and will can be distinguished in two ways. Intention concerns the nature of the result, while will concerns its actual existence. Intention can also mean a general resolve to act, while will means the resolve directed towards this particular act.

  564. If there really is a distinct state of the human soul between firm knowledge and action, and we call it will, then it is an intention: an inward movement toward acting, like the natural tendency of a body to move from one place to another. It is not simply desire, even an intense desire, as will become clear. Nor is it knowledge. Love, dislike, satisfaction, anger, sorrow, joy, and other states of the soul all involve awareness, but that does not make them identical with knowledge. If will is a separate state coming between our knowledge and what we do, it cannot itself be our knowledge.

    This also shows why removing the limits of human will does not turn its meaning into God's knowledge. The very ideas are different. By contrast, when we remove the limits of human knowledge, we can still keep its basic meaning: something being present to a knower. Even if we take away every feature that makes it a temporary human mental state, that meaning survives. In the case of will and knowledge, however, stripping away limitations cannot make two different meanings identical.

    If we attribute will to God after removing those limitations, we should therefore understand it as a quality shown in His actions, as we do with creating, bringing into being, and showing mercy. When an act has everything necessary for its completion, we can call it willed from the side of the act and say that God wills it from the side of its source. Similarly, what sustains a thing in existence is its provision: the thing is provided for, and God is the Provider. The Qur'an commonly speaks of will in this way: “We wished to favor those who were made weak in the land”; “Your Lord wished that they should reach maturity”; “Who could prevent God if He wished to destroy the Messiah?”; and “When He wills a thing, His command is only to say to it, ‘Be,’ and it is.” Other verses follow the same pattern.

    What the author and other philosophers say about an eternal will belonging to God's essence is true in what it intends to establish. They have arguments for it. Yet those arguments show that everything apart from God depends on His power—the unrestricted source of all good—and on His knowledge of the order of goodness. They do not show that the word will, once purified of human limits, means the same thing as His knowledge of what is best, or that its meaning can be applied to the knowledge that is identical with His essence.

    It has indeed been proved that God possesses every perfection of being. But that is not by itself a reason to single out will as a separate name among His essential attributes. The philosophers' point is sound in substance. The remaining dispute concerns which word properly expresses it and whether the meaning drawn from our experience of willing can be applied to God's knowledge. As you can see, this is largely a question about language. — Ṭ. M.

    — ط مد ظله

  570. We explained earlier that an act performed under compulsion can still be an act of will. The person who compels someone acts upon the knowledge that comes before the will, not upon the will considered by itself. Without willing, the act would not be the person's act at all.

If, however, someone threatens to kill the person unless they climb down, and they climb down, that descent is compelled but still willed. If they climb down without any threat because they decide to do so, they act both willingly and freely.

    The difference between a forced act and a freely chosen act is not the presence of will in one and its absence in the other. It is whether the act agrees with or goes against the person's own aims. It gives a strong account of both sides of the question: the natural world begins again and again and never stands still, while God's gift of existence never runs out and His words are never exhausted.   594. The necessity mentioned in the objection is necessity in itself. If the world's coming into existence were necessary in itself, there would be more than one being necessary in itself, which is impossible. Nor can this necessity simply be the necessity of God's own essence: the argument describes it as something understood in relation to another, whereas God's essence is not dependent on any such relation.

    Perhaps the intended claim is that the world's existence is necessary through God's necessity. The author earlier distinguished this from a thing being made necessary by His action. Or perhaps it means necessity in relation to God: as God is necessary in Himself, He is necessary in relation to the world as a whole, and the first thing that comes from Him is necessary in relation to Him.

    Another reply is to distinguish the two sides of coming into existence. In its relation of dependence on God, the world's existence is necessary, because the One whose existence is necessary lacks no perfection. Considered as the world's own existence, it is possible in itself. The same coming into existence can thus be necessary from the side of its cause and possible from the side of its effect.

  596. The sound meaning of “a position between the two” is this: causing and bringing things into being depend on existence. Nothing acts before it exists. Every existence, whether of a cause or an effect, has a relation to God when considered apart from the separate essences to which we give names. In that respect, the effects of created existence are effects of God's existence. But existence also has a relation to the essences of created things; in that respect they have their own effects, just as they have their own existence.

    If we look at existence in its necessary dependence on God, we speak of all things being under His power. This is the oneness of acts grounded in the oneness of His essence and attributes. It is not the fatalist's account, which speaks of the oneness of acts while leaving the oneness of God's reality unexplained. An effect points us back to its source.

    If, instead, we look at existence as belonging to possible things, we speak of choice and action. A person who understands both sides does not erase either of them.

    Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī's distinction between first and immediate causes can be read in this way. We could even reverse the description while keeping its point: seen as God's, existence displays the action of the one who freely wills; seen as belonging to creatures, it shows their dependence on a creator whose power rules over them. The first explanation is easier to grasp. The second makes a subtler distinction.

  619. The author speaks of something “smokelike,” although the usual older medical term is the vapour-like spirit. He has already connected the two descriptions. This could be because the heavens are like a subtle, smokelike spirit in the body of the greater world; or because the heaven of the smaller world, the human being, is the vapour-like spirit.

    The “layers” of this spirit refer to three kinds recognized in the old medical account. The brain has a spirit concerned with perception and the nerves are its channels. The heart has the vital spirit, carried through the arteries. The liver has the natural spirit, carried through the veins.

    On this account, the spirit associated with the brain is finer and higher than that of the heart, and the heart's is finer than the liver's. Even within the brain, its rear part is said to be finer than its middle, and the middle finer than its front. The same ordering can be drawn within the front part. These are features of the historical theory, not present-day anatomy.
